summary: ENH: optimize: added "revised simplex" for scipy.optimize.linprog
description:
This PR adds the method `'revised simplex'` to `linprog`. Advantages:

- More accurate than method `'interior-point'`
- Much faster and more robust than method `'simplex'` (see benchmarks in #9636)
- Amenable to a sparse implementation and many other improvements
- Basic feasible solutions returned by simplex methods are often preferred for sensitivity analysis
- There are very effective warm-start methods for simplex methods, making them better suited than interior-point methods for use in mixed integer programming

This PR also:

- improves the appearance and clarity of the [`linprog` documentation](https://10639-1460385-gh.circle-artifacts.com/0/html-scipyorg/generated/scipy.optimize.linprog.html#scipy.optimize.linprog),
- organizes and strengthens the `linprog` test suite, and
- adds callback function support to methods `'interior-point'` and `'revised simplex'` equivalent to existing support in `'simplex'`.

The new method has been benchmarked extensively (see #9636) and all previous and new unit tests are passing (one failure due to Pocketfft).

---
Originally 9/12/2018:

Added a revised simplex method to `scipy.optimize.linprog`.

For now, `simplex` should remain the default method thanks to @Kai-Striega working the bugs out and this one still struggles a bit with some of those hard problems. But I think that this can serve as the foundation for a future default method for `linprog`. The advantage over the interior point method is that the solutions are basic, which can be useful for applications like sensitivity analysis and (eventually) mixed integer linear programming. The advantage over the existing simplex method will be speed (untested) and (eventually) support for sparse matrices.

One known bug is that when artificial columns remain in the basis of the solution to the phase one problem, nothing is stopping them from being replaced by columns that make the basis singular. I am still considering the most elegant way to fix that. This is the cause of the numerical difficulties in `test_bug_6690` and `test_bug_8662`. 
*Update 9/14/18*: Fixed. See loop in `_get_more_basis_columns`. Suggestions for more elegant solution welcome.
*Update 1/6/19*: Re-fixed a few weeks ago. I misunderstood the procedure for driving artificial variables out of the basis in the original implementation, and the randomized hack from 9/14/18 can be problematic. The new fix is a standard procedure, but the current implementation is quite slow because a) the basis matrix is factored from scratch for each artificial variable left in the basis and b) all rows of B^-1 A are calculated rather than just the one corresponding with the artificial variable being driven out. This could be improved with some extensions to the `BGLU` class.

This method still lacks support for callback and a 'display' option. *UPDATE 12/23/18* Added both.

Implementation details: rather than performing elementary row operations on a full tableau, the "vanilla" revised simplex method maintains an inverse of the basis matrix, efficiently applying updates to this inverse each iteration of the algorithm. (This is possible because only one column of the basis matrix is changed per iteration.) However, matrix inversion is not numerically stable, so this implementation uses a matrix factorization (initially LU) and efficiently updates that (conceptually, by changing U and adding factors in-between L and U). The required elementary row operations have been Cythonized for speed. Eventually, the updated factorization can run into numerical issues, and so the basis matrix is factorized from scratch after a specified maximum number of iterations. Alternatively, there is an option to minimize the "amortized solve time". If enabled, the average time to solve  a linear system using the basis factorization is measured. Typically, the average solve time will decrease with each successive solve after initial factorization, as factorization takes much more time than the solve operation (and updates). Eventually, however, the updated factorization becomes sufficiently complex that the average solve time begins to increase. When this is detected, the basis is re-factorized from scratch.

*Update 9/15/18*: Performed some benchmarking on 80 of the Netlib problems (those on which dense presolve is practical; see #7123 for more information about these problems and graphs with interior-point and original simplex results). 

Reliability:
The dense interior point code solves all of these problems to reasonable accuracy, whether the default postsolve settings recognize it or not. (We might want to loosen these tolerances.) The revised simplex code currently solves 40 of them, whereas the old simplex code solves 14 with default settings. This might be improved by adjusting tolerances, as the old simplex code typically reports inability to find a BFS in phase 1. (Not that I recommend spending any time doing so.) There is one problem that the old simplex solver solves successfully that the revised simplex currently encounters numerical difficulties on.

Accuracy:
In the worst case, the interior point accuracy is not terrific; the objective function can be as much as 0.1% off the accepted value and still report success. There is almost always some measurable error in the objective function value, but it usually small (90th percentile value is ~0.0005%). The revised simplex code currently solves 40 of these problems and there is only measurable error in the objective for two, the worst of which is 0.00057%. There is no measurable error in any of the problems that the original simplex code solves.

Speed:
Without getting terribly specific, it's reasonable to say that for the problems revised simplex solves, revised simplex takes about 10x longer than interior point, and for the problems original simplex solves, original simplex takes about 2x longer than revised simplex. 
This is a little surprising. I expected revised simplex to be much more in line with the performance of interior point. This is because although simplex methods will typically take many more iterations than interior point, the time per iteration should be dramatically less. I think the two effects tend to cancel one another out in state of the art codes. This is not what I'm getting. The revised simplex method is actually taking about as long per iteration, on average, as interior point, and it is actually taking _longer_, on average, than original simplex. The time difference between original simplex and revised simplex is actually because revised simplex is finishing in far fewer iterations. This is particularly surprising, because the two simplex methods were supposed to be using the same pivoting rules! I'll have to look into that...

Summary:
Revised simplex is currently almost always superior in all performance categories to original simplex, but interior point is still the best of the lot by a large margin. I think we can improve the reliability of revised simplex considerably by adjusting the pivoting rules, as the numerical issues are always the result of pivoting to a singular basis, which isn't supposed to happen. The big question is whether we can get the time per iteration of the revised simplex code down. I was very careful in the implementation to keep the time per iteration down, as almost all the time writing this method was spent on the efficient factorization updates and Cythonizing that code. But now I suppose I know what I need to look into.

summary: EIGH very very slow --> suggesting an easy fix
description:
This post extends https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/7339, where @yaroslavvb noticed first that EIGH was surprisingly slow in Scipy vs Numpy.

Anyways first post on Scipy for me!!! Hi all!

I checked Scipy's code on EIGH and how it was implemented. Everything was fine, HOWEVER, you need to add 2 extra lines (literally) of code to make it approx 2-4 times faster than the old Scipy version, and even faster than Numpy's.

Scipy uses:
1. SYEVR if B = None and eigvals = None                  [Very slow non divide n conquer]
2. SYEVD if B = not None and eigvals = None           [Very Fasssttt divide n conquer]
3. SYEVX if B = not None and eigvals = not None.    [Slow as well]

There is a slight problem. It should be:
1. SYEVD if B = None (identity) and eigvals = None  [Very Fasssttt divide n conquer]
2. SYEVD if B = not None and eigvals = None           [Very Fasssttt divide n conquer]
3. SYEVX else

In other words, I propose that Scipy scraps SYEVR completely, and replaces everything with SYEVD. You can keep SYEVR for RAM constraining machines.

An easy fix I tried is:
```python
scipy.linalg.eigh(XTX, b = np.eye(len(XTX), dtype = X.dtype), turbo = True, check_finite = False)
```
Which performs at most 3-4 times faster than doing this:
```python
scipy.linalg.eigh(XTX, b = None, turbo = True, check_finite = False)
```
Note, I also tried:
```python
scipy.linalg.eigh(XTX, b = np.eye(len(XTX), dtype = np.int8), turbo = True, check_finite = False)
```
Which is even slower (meaning you must make identity same dtype as XTX

So, a simple fix in Scipy would be simply:
```python
def eigh(X, b.....):
    if b is None:
        b = np.eye(len(X), dtype = X.dtype)
    ....
```
In terms of timing, 
![image](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/danielhanchen/hyperlearn/master/Images/Preliminary%20Results%20N%3D5000%20P%3D6000.png)
Also, this post flows on from https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/11174, where I reported that PyTorch's SVD and GELS was slow and unstable.

summary: ENH: add capability to specify orders in pade func
description:
Currently interpolate.pade only takes the order of the denominator <m>
with the order of the numerator assumed from the order of the inputted
array <an>. Added an optional parameter <l> (following standard naming
convention of the pade function) which specifies the order of the
numerator. This is useful if the order of the inputted array returns
a higher order (and computationally more expensive) numerator than needed.
This change does not affect any currently written code.

summary: ENH: implement sparse matrix BSR to CSR conversion directly.
description:
The current implementation of sparse matrix BSR to CSR conversion is to convert to COO first, then to CSR. I noticed that there is a TODO in "scipy/sparse/bsr.py" to make the conversion more efficient. Also there is a half finished function template in "scipy/sparse/sparsetools/bsr.h". I have implemented direct conversion from BSR to CSR instead of converting via COO format. The direct conversion preserves now the (unsorted) block column indices and duplicated block columns.

There is a concern on the data copy of this conversion. Though the current function has a boolean argument to determine if the data are copied or not, the data are actually always copied. Mathematically, from BSR to COO we can avoid copy, but from COO to CSR the copy is almost inevitable, unless the block row size is one. Even in the current version of coo_matrix.tocsr, the data are always copied regardless of the input argument. For the direct conversion I keep the same way: there is a boolean argument, but the data are copied anyway.

P.S. this is the first time I submit a PR. I am not sure if I have done everything correctly, e.g. if the tests were well written and placed in correct position. I apologize for any mistakes.

description:
Previously, `cKDTree.query_ball_point()` would not sort the returned indices for single point queries, but did sort them for multi-point queries.

For multi-point queries with large numbers of returned indices, sorting slowed down `query_ball_point()` significantly.

Closes #8838

summary: BUG: Improve numerical precision/convergence failures of smirnov/kolmogorov
description:
Addresses #7426, #7455, #7456, #7492.

A rewrite of the algorithms in the Kolomgorov-Smirnov statistics package.

summary: ENH: small speedup for stats.gaussian_kde
description:
A 20% speedup in gaussian_kde.evaluate when the number of points is large (whether it is in the dataset, or the points on which the KDE is evaluated).

The speedup isn't huge, so I won't be offended if this is not merged :).

To benchmark, I adapted the example in the docstring:
```
import numpy as np
np.random.seed(42)

from scipy import stats
def measure(n):
    "Measurement model, return two coupled measurements."
    m1 = np.random.normal(size=n)
    m2 = np.random.normal(scale=0.5, size=n)
    return m1+m2, m1-m2


m1, m2 = measure(2000)
xmin = m1.min()
xmax = m1.max()
ymin = m2.min()
ymax = m2.max()


X, Y = np.mgrid[xmin:xmax:200j, ymin:ymax:200j]
positions = np.vstack([X.ravel(), Y.ravel()])
values = np.vstack([m1, m2])
kernel = stats.gaussian_kde(values)
```

Timing can then be done (in IPython):
`%timeit kernel(positions)`

With master, I get 2.17s, with this branch 1.73s.

summary: ENH: added association measurements Cramer's V, Tschuprow's T and Phi to scipy.contingency
description:
Added measures of association for nominal data to contingency stats module. Measures added include Tschuprow's T, Cramer's V and Phi. Measures are individual specified by values of the 'stat' argument (as 'T', 'V' or 'phi', respectively) within function scipy.stats.contingency.association_test.

These measures can provide useful information about variable independence to those performing chi-squared tests or categorical data analysis in general. Each of the measures is empirically estimated using the chi-squared statistic which, is automatically determined if the 'chi2_stat' argument is not specified. Also included is an option to apply a proposed method of bias correction developed by Bergsma (2013) [full reference included in code docs]. Lastly due to the measures requiring the specification of the number of rows and columns in the contingency table, a private function was added to reshape the any array that exceeded two dimensions to an N x N array. 

Tests were created for all included measures both with and without bias correction.

summary: ENH: Add shgo for global optimization of NLPs.
description:
Hello everyone.

As has been alluded to in previous e-mails to the SciPy mailing lists, we introduce the simplicial homology global optimisation (shgo) algorithm; a global optimisation (GO) algorithm written in pure Python (MIT license).

Introduction
----
shgo solves general black box problems of the following form:

       minimize f(x) subject to

       g_i(x) >= 0,  i = 1,...,m
       h_j(x)  = 0,  j = 1,...,p

where x is a vector of one or more variables.
   ``f(x)`` is the objective function ``f: R^n -> R``.
   ``g_i(x)`` are the inequality constraints ``g: R^n -> R^m``.
   ``h_j(x)`` are the equality constraints  ``h: R^n -> R^p``.


The project website provides a quick overview of the algorithm, it's usage and performance (and some aesthetically pleasing figures): https://stefan-endres.github.io/shgo/

Installation, usage and testing
---
The shgo module is published on PyPi under a MIT license and can be installed on your system for immediate use:

```$ pip install shgo```

The latest version can be cloned from this GitHub repository: https://github.com/Stefan-Endres/shgo

For a quick example using non-linear inequality and equality constraints see this subsection:
https://stefan-endres.github.io/shgo/#cattle-feed-hs73-problem-with-non-linear-constraints

As you can see the input is very similar to [`scipy.optimize.minimize`](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy-0.19.1/reference/generated/scipy.optimize.minimize.html) using the `SLSQP` method.

Note that while the test suite for shgo is relatively extensive and covers every method currently available in `scipy.optimize.minimize`, it is probably inevitable that there are many more bugs and issues that will arise. Aside from issues in this PR, please raise any issues on the [repository](https://github.com/Stefan-Endres/shgo) or e-mail them to me directly stefan.c.endres@gmail.com.

Performance
---
This link contains the performance profiles for shgo:
https://stefan-endres.github.io/shgo/#performance-summary

From the figures shgo compares very favourably to the other GO algorithms currently available in SciPy:
https://stefan-endres.github.io/shgo/#open-source-black-box-algorithms

Note that shgo is a deterministic algorithm so you should be able to replicate these results on your own system using the SciPy GO benchmarking suite. *Note, however, that 3 of these test problems take a very long time to run so I highly recommend using the `maxtime` option for shgo.* (I have never had a successful run with any of the other GO algorithms currently available in SciPy on these problems).

Further results against cutting edge blackbox GO algorithms that allow for constraints, also reveal a competitive performance for shgo. The algorithms in these tables were previously shown to be very competitive against the black box algorithms implemented in MATLAB. The MATLAB implementations were shown to have the best performance in an extensive study comparing a large number of popular and recent commercial and open source black box solvers (see this subsection for references to these publications):

https://stefan-endres.github.io/shgo/#recently-published-black-box-algorithms

Scope
---
As with most black box algorithms. The shgo is most algorithm is generally applicable to low dimensional black box problems ([~10-dimensional problems](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fhNuspYbMeI)) unless more information can be supplied to the algorithm. This is not necessarily only gradients and hessians. For example, if it is known that the decision variables of the objective function are symmetric, then the symmetry option can be used in order to solve problems with hundreds of variables.

Maintenance and further work
---
If accepted into SciPy the code will be maintained there and/or in the PyPi module by [me](https://github.com/Stefan-Endres/shgo) and [my adviser](https://github.com/alchemyst). If shgo is wanted, I also assume there will be many additional changes requested, especially with respect to documentation, code style and additional unit tests in this PR.

Thank you for taking your time to read this PR.

summary: ENH: Wrap LAPACK's dsytrd
description:
This PR adds the wrapper for LAPACK's dsytrd, a routine that takes a real symmetric matrix A and transforms it to a tridiagonal matrix by an orthogonal similarity tranformation
```
Q^T * A * Q = T
```
With test.

I would have wrapped its complex variant `*HETRD` as well, but I didn't know how to map the complex type `<ctype2c>` to its corresponding real type in the wrapper code. (`HETRD` transforms a _complex_ Hermitian matrix to a _real_ symmetric tridiagonal matrix.)

Fixes #7775.

summary: Adaptive Nelder-Mead
description:
A small suggestive addition for the Nelder-Mead algortihm.

This paper [Sec 4.1] https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007%2Fs10589-010-9329-3 describes how adapting the step-parameters to the dimensionality of the problem at hand improves performance, especially for high-dimensional problems.
This pull request adds this as an option with the optional adaptive=True/False argument.

I don't know if this is something that is wanted in scipy, but I'm using this version myself, and so I thought I'd make a pull request.

summary: WIP: ENH: Polygon Surface Area Calculation
description:
### Purpose
To allow users to (rapidly) calculate the surface areas of polygons that lie in the plane (i.e., from `scipy.spatial.Voronoi`) or on the surface of a sphere (i.e., from `scipy.spatial.SphericalVoronoi`).

### Background
There are a number of ways to calculate the areas. Many approaches for the spherical polygons suffer from precision issues with angle calculations. You can find some discussion of the early work we tried in the issue motivating this PR: #6069

A [NASA JPL white paper](https://trs-new.jpl.nasa.gov/bitstream/handle/2014/40409/JPL%20Pub%2007-3%20%20w%20Errata.pdf?sequence=3&isAllowed=y) describes a nice way to perform the surface area calculation both in the plane and on the surface of a sphere. It is their approach that forms the starting point for the implementation in this PR. [Other approaches](http://mathworld.wolfram.com/SphericalPolygon.html) will be / have been used for i.e., unit testing. 

### Current State of the Code and Limitations
 - simple unit tests are passing for planar & spherical triangles now (with both CW & CCW vertex sort order)
   - need to start thinking about more convoluted test cases
       -  complicated planar & spherical polygons -- both convex & concave, with known areas
       - planar polygons containing one or more holes (will we support these?)
       - spherical polygons containing one or more holes -- see: Bevis and Cambareri (1987) Mathematical Geology 19
 - major issue now -- spherical polygons which include a pole or encompass an entire hemisphere or more -- these seems to be a special case which can't be handled by the area integration approach used in the JPL paper, which is probably why they explicitly excluded polar inclusion in any input polygons
   - special casing a subset of input spherical polygons could make vectorization of code much more difficult (on top of the fact that polygons can have differing numbers of vertices)
 - unit tests are now also passing for the draft cythonized version of the code, though I note that there is no [real performance benefit](https://github.com/tylerjereddy/bench_SA_scipy/blob/master/bench_scipy_surface_area.ipynb) in the plane or on the sphere yet; these are, however, serial implementations that may eventually be useful for comparison with vectorized approaches
  - need to decide if we'd require spherical input to be on the same sphere (and would this enable a substantial performance improvement)?
  - currently using the [hypothesis](https://hypothesis.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) testing library, but this may not fly if the code is to be merged in some day -- idea is just to probe the limitations as harshly as possible for now, especially given that the spherical results are formally an approximation

### Who is currently working on this?
 - I'm trying to chip away at it along with @james-nichols, a mathematician in France

### Related issues
 - it is still challenging to [plot spherical polygons in Python](https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/pull/6248)

### Some (vectorized) algorithm notes / potential plans (rough)
  - input: a list of numpy arrays containing the ordered spherical polygon vertex coordinates in Cartesian space; i.e.: [ [poly_1], [poly_2], ..., [poly_N] ]
     - the data structure is 'heteogeneous' (the polygons can have different array shapes) so direct application of numpy ufuncs is not immediately possible 
  - "fill" the input data structure with i.e., None / nan values using the largest polygon shape as the lowest common denominator; so if the largest polygon has 9 vertices, would end up with an array of shape: (N_polygons, 9, 3)
  - convert the array of homogenously-shaped / None-filled data to latitude / longitude coord format
  -  use ufunc operations to calculate area: array_edge_areas (data_array[...,1:,0] - data_array[...,:-1,0]) * (2. + np.sin(data_array[...,:-1,1]) + np.sin(data_array[...,1:,1]) )
       - doesn't this fail to complete the cycle though? have to think carefully about the end / start of the polygon and whether or not I can get away with a ufunc-style operation for this ***
        - array_edge_areas should have shape: (N_polygons, area_under_each_edge, 1) or similar -- can reshape to this if needed since order should be preserved
        - again note that areas will have to have been calculated either CW or CCW
  - np.sum() across the appropriate axis to sum together the signed areas calculated above
    - this should produce the actual polygon areas with array_areas having shape: (N_polygons,)

summary: ENH: add n-dimensional DCT and IDCT to fftpack
description:
I recently needed an n-dimensional `dct` and `idct`.  This PR adds these.  

The implementation is trivial, as the existing 1D routines already had `axis` support, but I thought it may still be worth providing.

description:
I have implemented the iterative trust-region algorithm described in the book ["Trust region methods" (Conn, Gould and Toint, 2000) pp.169-200 ](http://epubs.siam.org/doi/book/10.1137/1.9780898719857) 

The advantage of this method is that it can provide a much more accurate solution for the trust-region subproblem than, for instance, the dogleg method.  For each iteration it solve the trust-region subproblem iteratively requiring typically three Cholesky factorizations (agaist the single Cholesky factorization needed by dogleg method).

For alternative references: this algorithm is also described in ["Numerical Optimization" (Nocedal and Wright, 2006) pp.83-91](http://home.agh.edu.pl/~pba/pdfdoc/Numerical_Optimization.pdf) and, a variation of it, in the paper ["Computing a Trust Region Step" (Moré and Sorensen, 1983)](http://cds.cern.ch/record/136890/files/CM-P00069193.pdf).

summary: WIP: ENH: Integrating LAPACK "expert" routines with conditioning warnings for linalg.solve_ family
description:
As briefly discussed in #6634, in this PR the ?GESVX routine of LAPACK is exposed for generic use. They are the so-called eXpert versions of the already existing ?GESV routine family which are used in `sp.linalg.solve` 

The use case for these routines are many-fold 
- The most important case is to finally change the silent singular matrix handling. With the condition number and error estimates, a warning/error/msg can be emitted (needs-decision).
- Ill-conditioned matrices can be checked before inversion steps and nonsensical results can be avoided
- cond and rcond functions can now use estimates for comparison
- the lu factorization comes with a bonus (as is with ?GESV too but the API throws it away currently)
- The numerical accuracy is improved thanks to the balancing and iterative refinement (Lapack prefers the term `equilibration` for this particular instance). 

The API requirements for such routine is a bit tedious to satisfy. One of the main reasons for that is the variety of options to choose from. To give an example, here is an example from LAPACK documentation: 

> ```
>      EQUED is CHARACTER*1
>       Specifies the form of equilibration that was done.
>       = 'N':  No equilibration (always true if FACT = 'N').
>       = 'R':  Row equilibration, i.e., A has been premultiplied by
>               diag(R).
>       = 'C':  Column equilibration, i.e., A has been postmultiplied
>               by diag(C).
>       = 'B':  Both row and column equilibration, i.e., A has been
>               replaced by diag(R) * A * diag(C).
>       EQUED is an input argument if FACT = 'F'; otherwise, it is an
>       output argument.
> ```

or an even more joyful one is the following 

> ```
>       AF is DOUBLE PRECISION array, dimension (LDAF,N)
>       If FACT = 'F', then AF is an input argument and on entry
>       contains the factors L and U from the factorization
>       A = P*L*U as computed by DGETRF.  If EQUED .ne. 'N', then
>       AF is the factored form of the equilibrated matrix A.
> 
>      If FACT = 'N', then AF is an output argument and on exit
>       returns the factors L and U from the factorization A = P*L*U
>       of the original matrix A.
> 
>      If FACT = 'E', then AF is an output argument and on exit
>       returns the factors L and U from the factorization A = P*L*U
>       of the equilibrated matrix A (see the description of A for
>       the form of the equilibrated matrix).
> ```

There will be a a few phases for this PR to come to fruition and I would really appreciate all the feedback from the wizards.
- [x] Make sure the f2py interface is correct. 
- [x] Make sure that the input-output arguments are handled correctly.
- [x] Make sure that the varying number of I/O arguments are not exposed to the user and the decision tree should not lead to confusion. In other words, if out of inexperience a user selects two conflicting keyword arguments (as it is extremely easy to fall into those traps) the behavior should be unambiguous override or err out directly. 
- [ ] Make sure that the tests cover sufficient examples
- [x] Decide on the numerical bound formula to accept numerical singularity
- [ ]  Decide on where this functionality goes into, existing `sp.linalg.solve` as an addition or a standalone solver and so on.

I have adapted the matplotlib.mlab code for use in scipy.signal. This required rewriting welch to use the same underlying stride algorithm. 

Some reworking of the matplotlib code was needed to make functions work for
multidimensional arrays, as the current scipy.signal.welch function allows.
Things were also adjusted to keep the same welch API.

Advantages of this code change include:
- A speedup of about 8x in welch
- A speedup of about 6x in csd compared to extending the current

- Straightforward extensibility to add spectrogram functionality

There are probably still rough edges, but this seems to be working. Some

summary: ENH: scipy.signal - Cross Spectral Density and Coherence functions
description:

summary: Add Eigenvalue Range Functionality for Symmetric Eigenvalue Problems
description:
_Updated, renamed, and cleaned up. @apapanico 2016-08-25_
### Add Eigenvalue Range Functionality for Symmetric Eigenvalue Problems

This PR does the following:
- As discussed in  #6502, changes the interface the `-evr` LAPACK methods to allow for computing eigenvalues only in a half-open interval specified by the parameters `vl` and `vu`.
- As discussed in  #6502, backwards compatibility is ensured by further wrapping the `-evr` wrappers to reorder the arguments such that `vl` and `vu` come at the end of the optional argument list.   In `scipy/linalg/lapack.py`, the Fortran routines are wrapped after import and provided a new doc string to match the appropriate signature.  Moreover, a bug is addressed where `il` and `iu` are NOT properly ignored in `-evr` methods when not setting `range='I'` despite the claims of the LAPACK documentation.  For example, if `il` and `iu` are set to 1 and `range='A'`, then all eigenvalues are returned but only 1 eigenvector.  This is fixed by setting `il=1` and `iu = n` (the size of the matrix) when `range='A'` or `range='V'` so that there are no missing eigenvectors.  This approach is an improvement on #6503 which could not ensure a truly preserved ordering of input arguments.
- A new keyword argument, `eigrng`, is added to `scipy.linalg.eigh` that allows specifying this mode of use.  `eigrng` must be a tuple of length 2 and the first value must be less than the second value.  It cannot be specified in conjunction with `eigvals`.  Finally, the return values are all eigenvalues, and eigenvectors if desired, within the range.
- Tests are written that ensure the wrapper does not break backward compatibility, `eigh` functionality is as it should be, and that this new mode is incompatible with the mode specified by the parameter `eigvals` which computes eigenvalues corresponding to an index range.

summary: ENH: Add matrix normal distribution to stats
description:
I wrote a scipy-compatible implementation of the matrix normal distribution for a recent project. Would this be a good addition for the stats module?
### Some Notes
- The matrix normal distribution is useful for inference or sampling tasks involving unknown matrices. See e.g http://users.isy.liu.se/en/rt/schon/Publications/WillsSLN2012.pdf
- The matrix normal distribution generalises the multivariate normal distribution (because a vector is an `m x 1` matrix). However, separate implementations are appropriate because the vector case can be done more efficiently, and because the array dimensions would be different.
- Matrix normal sampling and pdf evaluation can be done by vectorising the `m x n` matrix into a `mn` vector and just using the vector distribution, and so implemented with a wrapper around the `multivariate_normal` classes. However, this is really inefficient, requiring us to handle a `mn x mn` covariance matrix. But it's useful for testing.
- Singular matrix normal distributions are well defined, but not supported here. They suffer from the same stability issues as the multivariate normal distribution. See https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/5286

Both allow to put emphasis on faster build time or faster query time and lower memory usage.
Since the `scipy.spatial.cKDTree` is the basis of the `scipy.interpolate.NearestNDInterpolator`, this possibility should also exist in `scipy.interpolate.NearestNDInterpolator`. For this, the constructor of `scipy.interpolate.NearestNDInterpolator` has been expanded by these parameters.

summary: Move lil_matrix storage to array.array for compatible data types.
description:
This PR changes the underlying storage of `lil_matrix` from Python `list` to `array.array` objects for compatible data types. For remaining data types, I continue to use plain lists.

This drastically reduces the amount of memory required for constructing a large `lil_matrix`.

With the current implementation:

```
Line #    Mem usage    Increment   Line Contents                
================================================                
     6     28.4 MiB      0.0 MiB   @profile                     
     7                             def example():               
     8                                                          
     9     28.4 MiB      0.0 MiB       shape = 1000, 1000       
    10                                                          
    11     36.0 MiB      7.6 MiB       arr = np.ones(shape)     
    12    104.0 MiB     67.9 MiB       mat = sp.lil_matrix(arr) 
```

Using arrays:

```
Line #    Mem usage    Increment   Line Contents               
================================================               
     6                             @profile                    
     7                             def example():              
     8    26.078 MB     0.000 MB                               
     9    26.078 MB     0.000 MB       shape = 1000, 1000      
    10                                                         
    11    33.723 MB     7.645 MB       arr = np.ones(shape)    
    12    57.246 MB    23.523 MB       mat = sp.lil_matrix(arr)
```

Since `list` and `array.array` support the same operations, this change should not break sensible user code that touches the `rows` and `data` attributes.

summary: ENH: optimize: add DF-SANE nonlinear derivative-free solver

Currently, the other large-scale derivative-free method offered in Scipy are Newton-Krylov and the Broyden/Anderson family. As one data point, solving a certain fixed-point integrodifferential equation problem, DF-SANE performed significantly better than the above solvers (NK was very slow as the Jacobian was 'difficult', Broyden/Anderson had problems in late-stage convergence).

In R, dfsane is implemented in the BB package, not sure how many other numerical computing environments include it.

Comments welcome.

summary: Pole placement
description:
Please find in this PR two pole placement algorithms for linear systems.

I started a code review topic for this on scipy-dev a few days ago and nobody raised any objections so I'm issuing a pull request. Please find below a cut'n paste of the code review request with explanations on what the code does and my concerns regarding licensing issues (it is really important to dig into these imho).

You will see that there are a lot of comments in the code, I hope they are not too verbose but I thought it was important to motivate every choice I made as the original publications are sometimes sloppy on details (see for example the choice of the initial transfer matrix X or what I do when an "improvement" on the transfer matrix yields a null vector, lines 1481 and 1175).

--- CUT'N PASTE STARTS HERE ---

As said a few days ago there are two algorithms, KNV method 0 (KNV0) and 
Yang Tits (YT). See code for urls to the reference papers.

Motivations for doing this in pure Python rather than linking some old 
fortran code:

I was in need of a 100% Python dependency free (except Numpy of course) 
pole placement function, integrating it into scipy was not my primary 
goal. Fortran code used for decades will for sure be faster and bug free 
but it was not an option.

Regarding KNV0:
- Licensing issues: I chose this method before knowing Matlab used it 
  too. I did read some old matlab source code (circa 2001 release iirc) at 
  the beginning of my work I won't lie on that, after Ralf Gommers warned 
  me it was not possible to port Matlab code I used my knowledge of their 
  code to stay as far as possible from what they did (the algorithm gives 
  some degrees of freedom). Given the current status of my code I can't 
  see any reason why it would be seen as a rip-off of their code unless 
  I'm banned from coding a projection into a vector space because I read 
  some Matlab code doing it. See lines 1171, 1172 and 1173 in ltisys.py 
  which are the core of this algorithm and are not in any way an idea 
  coming from Mathworks folks, these formulas are clearly written in the 
  reference publication page 1145 and 1146.
- Complex poles are not supported by the original algorithm. Using the 
  ideas from the second algorithm below I managed to reach a success rate 
  of 90% with complex poles but this is not reliable enough so the 
  relevant code is disabled. Matlab has a 100% success rate in their 2013 
  implementation but I don't know how they achieved that.

Regarding Yang Tits algorithm:
- This is an update of the KNV0 algorithm published in the mid 90's, as 
  far as I know it is only distributed by Slicot as "contributed MATLAB 
  functions" http://slicot.org/contributed-software under a non-free license.
- This implementation is 100% genuine, I did not read the code 
  distributed by slicot past the license header until my code was working 
  so there are no licensing issues imho. After achieving a working 
  implementation of this algorithm I checked the reference implementation 
  from Slicot and I'm still puzzled by how they did it. I'm sure there are 
  tons of good reasons why their implementation is faster/better than mine 
  but I simply can't understand what they did.
- Real poles are supported, sometimes the solution has a better 
  conditionning than KNV0's, sometimes not, but it does converge must 
  faster all the time. I was considering adding an option to return the 
  solution with the best conditionning from the two methods but it might 
  confuse users as it would only work on real poles. What do you think ?
- Complex poles are supported, I ran it for hours with random matrices 
  and poles and it never failed.

Please let me know if this code match you quality standards and I would 
really be glad if someone could test it and report any bug. The 
reference matlab implementations of these algorithms have been used and 
polished for decades, I'm sure I've missed lots of specific cases.

As a sidenote, if PR #4249 is accepted it should be possible to greatly 
improve the speed of these two algorithms.

summary: Add chirp Z-transform, zoom FFT
description:
As mentioned in numpy/numpy/issues/1177, Chirp Z-transform and special cases of it have been submitted to SciPy under public domain by Paul Kienzle and Nadav Horesh:  [[SciPy-user] Chirp Z transform](https://mail.python.org/pipermail/scipy-user/2009-January/019530.html) 

The special cases of CZT are zoom FFT and "scaled FFT" (not sure what that does).  DFT is also a special case of CZT, so if you call `czt(data)` with the default options, it's an FFT, but faster for prime sizes because of Bluestein's algorithm, useful in `resample` for instance? (#3956):

```
x = rand(42073) # prime length

allclose(czt(x), fft(x))
Out[37]: True

timeit czt(x)
10 loops, best of 3: 53.9 ms per loop

timeit fft(x)
1 loops, best of 3: 2.35 s per loop

2.35 / 53.9e-3 # speedup factor
Out[40]: 43.59925788497217
```

@stefanv said:

> Thank you both for the contribution!  I've reviewed the code and think
> it should be included in SciPy.  Would someone else like to have a
> look before I commit it?
> 
> Where would the best place for this be?  scipy.fftpack?

I think it makes sense to put it in scipy.fftpack, too, though that doesn't have any classes, just functions.  (Unless it should all be put in numpy, but I'm guessing zoom FFT is too specialized for that?)

summary: splprep works only up to 10 dimensional space
description:
If a b-spline curve in a space with more than 10 dimensions shall be approximated then splprep raises a TypeError.

Line 237 of scipy/interpolate/fitpack.py:

``` pyton
if not 0 < idim < 11:
    raise TypeError('0 < idim < 11 must hold')
```

I would expect the scipy documentation to mention this limitation. Therefore, I suggest updating
http://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy-0.14.0/reference/generated/scipy.interpolate.splprep.html#scipy.interpolate.splprep

Furthermore, a hint for finding a function that supports more than 10-dimensional space would be appreciated.

summary: ENH: Add second-order sections filtering
description:
With @endolith, we've put together a working version of second-order sections. Closes #2444.

This PR contains:
1. `sosfilt`, which performs filtering using second-order sections.
2. `zpk2sos` / `tf2sos` to convert to `sos` format. We might actually want to remove `tf2sos`. I'm worried that users might have filters in `tf` form and think that going to `sos` will reduce numerical error. Forcing them to do `zp2sos(tf2zpk(b, a))` might make them think twice about why there isn't a `tf2sos` function. I'm interested to hear other opinions on this...?
3. `cplxpair` and `cplxreal`, which are helper functions for dealing with complex conjugate pairings.

Implementing `filtfilt`-equivalent functionality should be very easy, but I think we should tackle that with #3259 as opposed to adding another function here.

One other thing missing is `lfiltic`-equivalent functionality. This will require some state-space gymnastics that I haven't managed to solve (despite some effort). I'll try to figure it out, but I think that could be left to a subsequent PR, especially since this one is already pretty big.

summary: ENH minimize, minimize_scalar: Add support for user-provided methods
description:
I'm using the excellent scipy.optimize infrastructure for research, experiments and benchmarking of some custom local minimization strategies. However, without this simple change, I have no easy way to plug my minimizer to basinhopping to overload it for global minimization as well; first I added a direct override possibility in PR #3321, but it has been pointed out that a more generic mechanism that could cover other cases would be nicer. A global registry of custom method names has been another idea, implemented in PR #3333 and it has its merits, but it has been deemed that overally a simpler and nicer way is simply passing a callable as the method parameter, instead of a string.

Therefore, this change does just that, checking if method is a callable instead of a string and in that case just going ahead and calling it - both in minimize and minimize_scalar of scipy.optimize.  It now also includes examples in the documentation and test suite checks.

scipy.linalg.eig does not handle infinite eigenvalues
description:
When a generalized eigenvalue problem `A*x=lambda*B*x` is solved, infinite eigenvalues may occur (if and only if `B` is singular). That's why the LAPACK function `ggev` (which is used by `eig`/`_geneig`) returns two scalars `alpha` and `beta` corresponding to each eigenvalue, see http://www.netlib.org/lapack/lug/node35.html. Three cases may occur
1. If `beta!=0` then `A*x=(alpha/beta)*B*x`.
2. If `alpha!=0` then `B*y=(beta/alpha)*A*y`.
3. If `alpha==beta==0` then the matrix pair `(A,B)` is singular, see http://www.netlib.org/lapack/lug/node105.html.

Currently `_geneig` divides by `beta` which may result in a division by zero. A simple example is

``` python
from scipy.linalg import eig
eig([[1]], [[0]])
```

This results in:

``` python
/usr/lib/python2.7/dist-packages/scipy/linalg/decomp.py:57: RuntimeWarning: divide by zero encountered in true_divide
  w = (alphar + _I * alphai) / beta
/usr/lib/python2.7/dist-packages/scipy/linalg/decomp.py:57: RuntimeWarning: invalid value encountered in true_divide
  w = (alphar + _I * alphai) / beta
Out[2]: (array([ inf+nanj]), array([[ 1.+0.j]]))
```

So this case needs some special treatment. Perhaps it's a good idea to return the `alphas` and `betas` and let the user decide how to proceed.

summary: distribution._stats is not vectorized
description:
discussed in PR gh-2849

two problems
- if moments and specific _stats are not available, then the generic calculation are not vectorize, if statements that assume scalar, and maybe other problems (no vec_moments ?)
- even if the distribution defines _stats that would work vectorized, the generic code has a bug 

(ignoring the first problem)
The second problem is because of the wrong calling sequence in stats, and I guess can be fixed relatively easily:

Warren's example

```
In [44]: invgamma.stats([0.0, 0.5, 1.0], 1, 0.5)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
ValueError                                Traceback (most recent call last)
<ipython-input-44-36163480f388> in <module>()
----> 1 invgamma.stats([0.0, 0.5, 1.0], 1, 0.5)

/home/warren/local_scipy/lib/python2.7/site-packages/scipy/stats/distributions.pyc in stats(self, *args, **kwds)
   1612                     mu = self._munp(1.0,*goodargs)
   1613                 out0 = default.copy()
-> 1614                 place(out0,cond,mu*scale+loc)
   1615                 output.append(out0)
   1616 

ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (3) (2) 
```

bug:
argsreduce is after the call to ._stats
a=0 is invalid shape parameter in Warren's example
._stats get's the full a (3 elements). When combining with loc and scale in line 1614, loc and scale only have valid args which means 2 elements in this case.

solution: argsreduce needs to go before ._stats.

some explanation
argsreduce is used in all methods to screen out invalid arguments and to broadcast the valid arguments to have common shape before calling the private methods.
The private .__xxx methods then only get valid arguments (that satisfy ._argcheck) and all arguments have the same shape.

In this case a=0 is removed (we set nans in the generic part), the two valid arguments together with loc and scale are broadcasted together.

In this case, the usage of argsreduce after the call to ._stats is screwed up.

We don't have currently any tests for `stats` with vectorized arguments, since this was not working. (enhancement not a bug)

summary: functions for testing minimization
description:
Would it be useful to gather some of these functions together?  I've noticed they are scattered across the scipy codebase.  I was thinking of something like a scipy/optimize/bench.py module to collect the functions, and add a few new ones.

The functions I have in mind would be smooth functions for minimization and would provide R^N -> R function evaluation, and also the gradient, the hessian, and an evaluation of the hessian-vector product for an arbitrary vector.

But the interface could become a little bit messy.  For example you might want to list one or more local or global mins or argmins for each function.  Maybe someone would also want the roots f(x)=0 when the function is R^1 -> R.  Furthermore, some functions (e.g. Rosenbrock) are parameterized R^N -> R where N can be specified by the user.  Some functions might have box constraints on their domains, or they might have more complicated domain constraints.

summary: Distributions: restrictions on parameter values at a lower level (Trac #1900)
description:
_Original ticket http://projects.scipy.org/scipy/ticket/1900 on 2013-04-24 by trac user Sytse, assigned to unknown._

A few recent tickets (gh-2399, gh-2402, gh-2414) show that restrictions on parameter values are not always properly specified. In the folded normal and the non-central t distributions they are not specified in an _argcheck() for the distribution class itself, but all parameter restrictions appear to be inherited as the restriction: 'par > 0' from a parent class 'rv_continuous' .

Although 'par > 0' is probably the most frequent restriction, it is not a fundamental restriction. I mean: there is no reason why in priciple all parameter values should be positive, except for a few. The decision to specify 'par > 0' in the parent classes and only to modify if necessary in the distribution classes may lead to unclarity and bugs at the distribution level. 

Wouldn't the design become clearer if no parameter restrictions were imposed on the parent level and all restrictions ('> 0', '>= 0', 'integer', etc) were defined explicitly for each distribution class separately?
No need to say in a Python environment that a clear and logical design is extremely important for readability and eventually for maintainability of code.

summary: trust region (Trac #1899)
description:
_Original ticket http://projects.scipy.org/scipy/ticket/1899 on 2013-04-23 by trac user unknown (google), assigned to @dlax._

Here's a trust region optimization code that I transcribed from chapter 4 of Nocedal and Wright Numerical Optimization (2nd edition).

It implements the "dogleg" trust region search strategy.  Currently the only optimization routine in scipy which explicitly makes use of the Hessian of the objective function is fmin_ncg which is based on line search and not on trust regions.  Although the dogleg search strategy is severely limited by its restriction to positive definite Hessian matrices, it might be helpful as a starting point for more practical methods.  For example, Matlab's default fmincon solver uses a trust region approach
http://www.mathworks.com/help/optim/ug/choosing-a-solver.html
and I don't think that fmincon is considered worse than Python's current solvers.

summary: LinearNDInterpolator fails when dimensions differ by many orders of magnitude (Trac #1666)
description:
_Original ticket http://projects.scipy.org/scipy/ticket/1666 on 2012-06-02 by trac user bloop369, assigned to unknown._

If I am calculating a function of two arguments, say f(t,x), LinearNDInterpolator fails when t and x differ by many orders of magnitude (like 15). Sometimes I get a QHull warning like:

qhull precision warning: 
The initial hull is narrow (cosine of min. angle is 1.0000000000000000). A coplanar point may lead to a wide facet.  Options 'QbB' (scale to unit box) or 'Qbb' (scale last coordinate) may remove this warning.  Use 'Pp' to skip this warning.  See 'Limitations' in qh-impre.htm.

In borderline cases, I get inaccurate results with no warning!

It is hardly unusual in science to have a function where one argument is many (ten or more) orders of magnitude larger than the other. For example, maybe I am calculating a function of time and space f(t,x) using SI units (seconds for t, meters for x), but I'm discussing astronomical phenomena or nanoscale phenomena or whatever.

Based on the warning message, it sounds like using the 'QbB' option ("scale to unit box") in QHull would be perfect to solve this problem. Is there any reason that this option is not used?

Sample code: x=1e-15;  points = np.array([[3_x,3],[3_x,5],[4_x,3],[4_x,5]]);  data = [4,5,6,7];  a = LinearNDInterpolator(points,data);  print a(3.5*x,4)

Mathematically, the answer should be 5.5, independent of x, but it fails when x is too big or small.

Thanks in advance!

summary: scipy.stats: inconsistent doc string (Trac #1650)
description:
_Original ticket http://projects.scipy.org/scipy/ticket/1650 on 2012-04-26 by trac user nicky, assigned to unknown._

The doc string on line (as of date April 16 2012) https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/master/scipy/stats/distributions.py#L129

to compute the moments of a distribution is like this: 

```
_doc_moment = \
"""moment(n, %(shapes)s, loc=0, scale=1)
    Non-central moment of order n
"""
```

Thus, a non-central moment should be returned.  On the other hand, the code on line 

https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/master/scipy/stats/distributions.py#L358

is as follows:

```
def _moment(data, n, mu=None):
    if mu is None:
        mu = data.mean()
    return ((data - mu)**n).mean()
```

This computes a central moment, not a non-central moment. 

Besides this, this code is called nowhere within distributions.py. Is it dead?

summary: Contingency Table Class (Trac #1258)
description:
_Original ticket http://projects.scipy.org/scipy/ticket/1258 on 2010-08-09 by trac user scopatz, assigned to unknown._

The attached files hold a new N-dimensional [http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contingency_table contingency table] class and tests for this class.  The standard two-way table is present in almost every elementary statistics book.  However, an adequate model has yet to be included in scipy.  

The class here allows the user to load a table from a numpy array.  Additionally, a contingency table can also be generated by sorting raw data from columns (1D arrays).

```
from scipy import stats
import numpy as np

# Initialize from array
obs = np.array([[10,0], [0, 10]])
ct = stats.ContingencyTable(observed=obs)

# Initialize from columns of data
a = np.array([1, 3,  10])
b = np.array([3, 60, 45])
c = np.array([0.9, 0.99, 0.999])
x = (a,b,c)

def nines(l, u, b):
    # Define our own distribution to apply to the data
    return 1.0 - np.logspace(np.log10(1.0 - l), np.log10(1.0 - u), b)

bounds = ([1, 10], [0, 2], [0.9, 0.999])
dists = (np.linspace, np.logspace, nines)

ct = stats.ContingencyTable.from_columns(x, shape=(2, 4, 3), 
    bounds=bounds, distribution=dists, discrete=(False, False, True))
```

Slices and summations of the contingency table are handled by class methods.  Additionally, important metrics, such as chi-squared value, entropy, and mutual information, are also defined as methods.

Note that one of the strengths of this implementation is that metrics of lower dimensionality can always be calculated using a combination of the above methods.  For example, using the 'from column' table above

```
# Entropy of original table, H(a,b,c)
h = ct.entropy

# Entropy of just the a and c axes, H(a, c)
ct1 = ct.collapse_shape((False, True, False))
h1 = ct1.entropy()
```

Some related tickets are [http://projects.scipy.org/scipy/ticket/893 893], [http://projects.scipy.org/scipy/ticket/956 956], and [http://projects.scipy.org/scipy/ticket/1203 1203]. 

Lastly, Warren Weckesser deserves a big thanks for working on this with me during the !SciPy 2010 statistics sprint.

summary: New regression test for reading compressed matlab streams. (Trac #918)
description:
_Original ticket http://projects.scipy.org/scipy/ticket/918 on 2009-04-11 by @thouis, assigned to unknown._

The test case, "test_skip_variable" in the included version of test_mio.py, demonstrates a bug in the 0.7.0 version of mio.mat_reader_factory that becomes apparent when you use the factory's get_variables method to skip over a first large, compressed variable to read a variable that appears after that variable.

This bug is no longer present in the current development tree.  This patch adds a regression test.  Lee Kamentsky discovered the bug, wrote the test case and had developed a patch relative to 0.7.0 (no longer relevant, but available if needed).

Below is the message from Lee describing the bug.

---

The test case, "test_skip_variable" in the included version of test_mio.py, demonstrates a bug in the mio.mat_reader_factory that becomes apparent when you use the factory's get_variables method to skip over a first large, compressed variable to read a variable that appears after that variable. The current code base misplaces the file object read location within the compressed variable's data rather than at its end, causing an exception when the code attempts to read the second variable.

I've got a distilled test case, scipy/io/matlab/tests/data/test_skip_variable.mat (20K), which is just barely large enough to trigger the bug (happens for compressed object > 16384).

The code:

273    def matrix_getter_factory(self):
274        __ Returns reader for next matrix at top level __
275        tag = self.read_dtype(self.dtypes['tag_full'])
276        mdtype = tag['mdtype'].item()
277        byte_count = tag['byte_count'].item()
278        if mdtype == miCOMPRESSED:
279            getter = Mat5ZArrayReader(self, byte_count).matrix_getter_factory()
280        elif not mdtype == miMATRIX:
281            raise TypeError, \
282                  'Expecting miMATRIX type here, got %d' %  mdtype
283        else:
284            getter = self.current_getter(byte_count)
285            next_pos = self.mat_stream.tell() + byte_count
286            getter.next_position = next_pos
287        return getter

For a compressed array, you enter this loop twice. The first time through, it reads the compression wrapper and, at line 279, it calls matrix_getter_factory again. This continues through line 284 to create the actual matrix reader and at line 286, it sets next_pos to the correct, uncompressed size. The code returns to line 279 and, in the old code, falls through to lines 286 (which was unindented in the old version) and mistakenly sets the getter next_position to the compressed size.

getter.next_position is used in miobase to in MatMatrixGetter.to_next() to advance past the object. There were no test cases of this function and the code would appear to work on small compressed objects of compressed size < 16384 because the entire object would be read and buffered. The test case included fails because it requires a second read to advance the stream.

def pascal(n):

    L_n = linalg.expm(diag(arange(1,n+1),-1))

summary: Statistics functions with new options (Trac #604)
description:
_Original ticket http://projects.scipy.org/scipy/ticket/604 on 2008-02-15 by trac user rspringuel, assigned to @cournape._

I created a personal statistics package because the functions already in scipy didn't satisfy the needs that I had.  In some cases this was because scipy's version didn't do what I wanted it to do, in other cases it was because scipy didn't have that function (or at least I couldn't find it if it did).  In those cases where scipy already had a version of the function, I tried to make my version capable of doing all the things that the scipy version could do, but since I code exclusively in python (I don't know any other coding languages) there were somethings that I couldn't implement (I couldn't modify the ndarray class, for instance, to make these methods of that class when numpy had that feature).

The features that I added because I needed them are as follows:
weights : of the statistical functions available, only average had the ability to incorporate weights.  All of my descriptive statistics functions have the ability to incorporate weights.  Where weights are not traditionally thought of, I started from the premise that in cases where all weights are whole numbers they should correspond to the frequency of observation for that particular data point.  E.g. unweighted statistics of the set [1,2,3,4,4,5,5,5] should have the same result as the set [1,2,3,4,5] with weights [1,1,1,2,3].  I've also included the ability to use ErrorVal, a package I found online, as the source for the weights, but mostly included that because I liked the idea behind ErrorVal when I found it.  Since writing that portion of the code I've found that I don't actually use ErrorVal all that much, so I wouldn't be adverse to editing that part of the code out if ErrorVal is not something that can be referenced for license reasons.

NaN handling: I needed the ability to specify how nan variables were handled in an array seperately from inf variables.  This is currently handled by having seperate functions for the nan friendly versions, some of which are buried in subpackages of stats.  I thought that this made them more difficult to use and so created my functions with a boolean flag that can set how nan variables are treated.

In addition to the descriptive statistics, I also filled out my package with some Goodness of Fit, Parameter, and Analysis of Residuals statistics.  These help with the post hoc analysis on an optimization solution for data.

by the same code below for trust-exact and trust-ncg.

import sys

import numpy as np

    def _minfunc(x):

def hessp(self, p):

```
def hessp(self, p):

summary: brentq can overflow / underflow
description:
According to the source code:

https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/5f4c4d802e5a56708d86909af6e5685cd95e6e66/scipy/optimize/Zeros/brentq.c#L67

the brentq algorithm uses the product of two function values to see if the zero is in the bracketing interval.

In 

    Malcolm, Michael A., Cleve B. Moler, and George Elmer Forsythe. 
    Computer methods for mathematical computations. Prentice-Hall, 1977.

we see the following advice:

"Careful attention is paid to underflow and overflow problems. For example, the test to ensure that F(B) and F(C) have different signs is *not* the conventional:

F(B) * F(C) < 0.0

If F(B)=10^-40 and F(C)=10^-40, then they have opposite signs, but on many computers the product will underflow and be set to zero, and the test will fail."

summary: Sparse matrix argmax() integer overflow on Windows 10
description:
When running on Windows 10, the sparse.csc_matrix.argmax() function can silently overflow the int data type and return the wrong value with sufficiently large matrices. This issue does not occur on Linux.

#### Reproducing code example:

```
import numpy
from scipy import sparse

dim = (100000, 100000)
mat = sparse.lil_matrix(dim)
mat[99998, 99998] = 1
mat = sparse.csc_matrix(mat)

idx = mat.argmax()
idx_unravelled = numpy.unravel_index(idx, dim)

print(idx_unravelled)
print(mat[idx_unravelled])
print(mat[99998, 99998])
```

Expected output:

```
(99998, 99998)
1.0
1.0
```

Actual output:

```
(14099, 65406)
0.0
1.0
```

Workaround:

```
maxval = mat.max()
if idx < 0:
    idx += 1 << 32
idx_unravelled = numpy.unravel_index(idx, dim)
while mat[idx_unravelled] < maxval:
    idx += 1 << 32
    idx_unravelled = numpy.unravel_index(idx, dim)

print(idx_unravelled)
print(mat[idx_unravelled])
```

#### Scipy/Numpy/Python version information:
```
1.6.1 1.18.4 sys.version_info(major=3, minor=8, micro=5, releaselevel='final', serial=0)
```

Again, I am only having this problem on Windows. The same code runs with SciPy 1.6.1 on Ubuntu 20.04 with no problem.

Median-averaging of complex CSDs
description:

Note: This is a comment, and won't appear in the output.

`signal.csd` does not median-average complex CSDs correctly because of unexpected behavior of `np.median` for complex-valued arrays (see [the numpy issue](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/12943)). [Line 589 of signal/spectral.py](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/master/scipy/signal/spectral.py#L589) could be modified so that if the CSD is complex, its real and imaginary parts are separately median-averaged.

#### Reproducing code example:
<!-- 
If you place your code between the triple backticks below, 
it will be rendered as a code block. 
-->

```
import numpy as np
from scipy import signal

s = 0.3 * np.random.uniform(size=100000) # white noise
n1 = np.random.uniform(size=100000)
n2 = np.random.uniform(size=100000)
d1 = s + n1
d2 = s + n2
freq, Pss = signal.csd(s, s, nperseg=100) # mean average PSD of s
_, Pssmed = signal.csd(s, s, nperseg=100, average='median') # median average PSD of s
_, P12 = signal.csd(d1, d2, nperseg=100) # mean average CSD of d1 and d2
_, P12med = signal.csd(d1, d2, nperseg=100, average='median') # median average CSD of d1 and d2
```

The real and imaginary parts of `P12` should have similar variances, but in the median-averaged case the variance of the imaginary portion is much too high.

summary: BUG: Explicit dtype specification in _upfirdn.py
description:
Issue: By default, the shape of the output array created by `scipy.signal.upfirdn` was specified by an array with the default `dtype` of  `np._int`, which on some platforms is equal to `np.int32`. As a result, `upfirdn` would fail when passed a (large) signal array `x` if any dimension had length > 2^32-1.

#### Reference issue
Closes #11128.

#### What does this implement/fix?
This fix explicitly sets the `dtype` of the array which specifies the shape of the array returned by `upfirdn` to `np.int64`.

#### Additional information
See https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/9464 for additional details.

summary: BUG: wrong weights of the 7-point gauss rule in QUADPACK: dqk15w.f
description:
### Describe your issue.

QUADPACK: dqk15w.f: line #103, wrong weights of the 7-point gauss rule
The weights of wg should be the same as "dqk15.f":
#103: "0.3818300505051889d+00", should be changed to "0.3818300505051189d+00".

My issue is about a possible memory leak in scipy.spatial.distance.pdist and scipy.spatial.distance.cdist

#### Reproducing code example:
<!--

it will be rendered as a code block.

```
import numpy as np
from scipy.spatial.distance import pdist
X = np.random.uniform(0, 100, size=10000).reshape(-1, 10)
for _ in range(10000):
    test = pdist(X/0.01, metric='sqeuclidean')
    
```

#### Error Description:
On my Mac OSX 10.14.6 the memory consumption of the snipped above quickly rises into the Gigabytes (after a few seconds). If I remove the division from the pdist argument (see below), the problem vanishes. (I don't think this is intended behavior, as it also leads to excessive memory consumption in the Gaussian Process Regression implementation of Sklearn, where they have a similar line in the implementation of the RBF kernel)

The code, which does not produce this problem (division removed):
```
import numpy as np
from scipy.spatial.distance import pdist
X = np.random.uniform(0, 100, size=10000).reshape(-1, 10)
for _ in range(10000):
    test = pdist(X, metric='sqeuclidean')

summary: BUG: n-d interpolation parameter provided to geometric_slerp
description:
This was first reported by @BvB93 during addition of type hints to the related code.

In short, [`geometric_slerp()`](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.spatial.geometric_slerp.html) was intended to be a bit like `np.linspace` on the surface of an n-dimensional circle/sphere, interpolating between start and end points on that surface. However, it somehow slipped through that we allow arbitrary dimensions for the interpolation points/array, and this leads to weird/inconsistent/incorrect results.

Examples are below, where the "intended" 1-dimensional case produces the correct output--two points with 1 in the middle of the unit circle between the start/end. Notice the confusing discrepancy between the degenerate path output shapes vs. non-degenerate. While the non-degenerate outputs respect the input shape for `ndim > 1`, their numerical results are incorrect--the `x` coordinate isn't reflecting the movement along the unit circle to the halfway point between `[0, 1]` and `[1, 0]`.

What I'd like to do is raise an exception if `np.asarray(t).ndim > 1` and just move on, but as Bas points out we do have *de facto* support (no error raised) for arbitrary dimensions whether I like it or not, and I don't want my own view on it to exempt it from backwards compatibility concerns. That said, I wonder if we can basically say that this is a clear bug so it trumps backward compatibility?

```python
import numpy as np
import scipy
from scipy.spatial import geometric_slerp

print("scipy.__version__:", scipy.__version__)

arr1 = np.array([0, 1])
arr2 = np.array([1, 0])

for t in [[0, 0.5],
          [[0, 0.5]],
          [[[[[[[[[0, 0.5]]]]]]]]]]:
    print("t dims:", np.asarray(t).ndim)
    path = geometric_slerp(start=arr1,
                           end=arr2,
                           t=t)
    print("path:\n", path)
    degenerate_path = geometric_slerp(start=arr1,
                                      end=arr1,
                                      t=t)
    print("degenerate_path:\n", degenerate_path)
```

```
scipy.__version__: 1.8.0.dev0+1472.130a1e6
t dims: 1
path:
 [[0.         1.        ]
 [0.70710678 0.70710678]]
degenerate_path:
 [[0. 1.]
 [0. 1.]]
t dims: 2
path:
 [[[0.         0.70710678]]]
degenerate_path:
 [[0. 1.]
 [0. 1.]]
t dims: 9
path:
 [[[[[[[[[[0.         0.70710678]]]]]]]]]]
degenerate_path:

description:

My issue is about the documentation of lagrange interpolation here: https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.interpolate.lagrange.html
lagrange returns a numpy.poly1d  that contains "The polynomial’s coefficients, in decreasing powers"

Then, the documentation shows to pass this result to numpy Polynomials. But this class accepts as parameters "Polynomial coefficients in order of increasing degree"
https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.polynomial.polynomial.Polynomial.html

Does it seem like a conceptual error?
Coefficients are the same, but the order is reversed so when you want to interpolate things do not work well

#### Reproducing code example:
```
from numpy.polynomial.polynomial import Polynomial
from scipy.interpolate import lagrange
x = np.array([0, 1, 2])
y = x**3
poly = lagrange(x, y)

poly1d([ 3., -2.,  0.]) #3x^2 -2x

Polynomial(poly).coef
array([ 3., -2.,  0.]) #-2x +3
```



#### Scipy/Numpy/Python version information:

```
import sys, scipy, numpy; print(scipy.__version__, numpy.__version__, sys.version_info)
1.7.0 1.20.3 sys.version_info(major=3, minor=7, micro=3, releaselevel='final', serial=0)

summary: csgraph.maximum_flow can cause Python crash for large but very sparse matrices
description:
While reviewing #14358, I ran into the following issue (which affects both the implementation in that PR and the currently available SciPy implementation):

#### Reproducing code example:

Consider the flows calculation of the following very simple graph (in which each vertex has exactly one successor), represented by the matrix with ones on the superdiagonal and zeros elsewhere:

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.sparse import csr_matrix
from scipy.sparse.csgraph import maximum_flow

def calc_flow(n):
    indices = np.arange(1, n)
    indptr = np.array(list(range(n)) + [n - 1])
    data = np.ones(n - 1, dtype=int)
    A = csr_matrix((data, indices, indptr), shape=(n, n))
    return maximum_flow(A, 0, n - 1)
```

On my machine, running this for `n in (10, 100, 1_000, 10_000)`, I get the expect result (a flow of 1), but for `n = 100_000`, Python crashes. This seems to suggest faulty memory allocation somewhere in the preprocessing for the flow calculation; the graph itself is so small that performing the calculation should be unproblematic.

#### Scipy/Numpy/Python version information:

```
1.6.1 1.19.2 sys.version_info(major=3, minor=7, micro=6, releaselevel='final', serial=0)
```

summary: BUG: Reference count leak in distance_pybind
description:
#### Reference issue
Fixes #14382

#### What does this implement/fix?
These `PyArray_FromAny` wrappers were using `reinterpret_borrow` which actually increments the refcount on the array, and in this case leaks the original reference. Instead, we need `reinterpret_steal` which just wraps the object without increasing the reference count, then the original reference is managed automatically.

summary: BUG: KDTree balanced_tree is unbalanced for degenerate data
description:
#### Reference issue
Fixes gh-14074

#### What does this implement/fix?
The `balanced_tree` argument is meant to create a more balanced tree by splitting at the median instead of the midpoint of the known bounds. However, the "sliding" part of the sliding midpoint rule was also being applied after choosing the median which results in an unbalanced split for degenerate data. Instead, keeping it as the exact median results in a balanced tree.

#### Additional information
The comments state the median rule comes from sklearn, and this is equivalent to KDTree code:
https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/3ae7c7615343bbd36acece57825d8b0d70fd9da4/sklearn/neighbors/_binary_tree.pxi#L1176-L1181

cc @sturlamolden @rainwoodman

summary: BUG: medfilt can access beyond the end of an array
description:
#### Reference issue
Should fix #14273 (don't have a local windows build to confirm though)

#### What does this implement/fix?
`compare_functions` is an array of size `NPY_NTYPES`. NumPy has since added new type codes for datetime, timedelta and float16. For these three types the code would access beyond the end of the array. If that static data happens to contain zeroes we are okay, if not it may interpret some random data as a function pointer and call it as if it were the comparison function.

summary: BUG: Fixed an issue wherein `SphericalVoronoi` could raise for certain array-likes
description:
#### Reference issue
n.a.

#### What does this implement/fix?
`SphericalVoronoi` would previously assume that the passed `points` (a 2D array-like) would support `__getitem__`.
While this is true for majority of cases (_i.e._ ndarrays or nested sequences), this assumption does not necessarily 
hold true for others, including the likes of memoryviews or objects that only implement the `__array__` protocol.

Aforementioned issue has been resolved by removing the getitem operation on the `points` array-like,
instead extracting the relevant axis length from its corresponding ndarray.

summary: BUG: Fixed an issue wherein `geometric_slerp` would return an incorrect shape/type for degenerate inputs
description:
#### Reference issue
n.a.

#### What does this implement/fix?
Whenever the `start` and `end` parameters of `geometric_slerp` were degenerate, the function would previously return a list of length `t.size` filled with views of `start`.

There are a number of problems with this approach:
* It completely ignores the shape of `t`; this code-path thus ignores any broadcasting that would otherwise occur.
* All of a sudden a list is returned where one would expect an array.
* All list elements were, in fact, the very same array, potentially the same array the user previously passed as input. 
  This an excellent way for unexpected bugs to sneak into user code.

#### Additional information
The behavior prior to this PR:
``` python
In [1]: from scipy.spatial import geometric_slerp

In [2]: geometric_slerp([0, 1], [0, 1], t=[0, 0.5])  # degenerate `start` and `end`
Out[2]: [array([0., 1.]), array([0., 1.])]

In [3]: geometric_slerp([0, 1], [1, 0], t=[0, 0.5])  # non-degenerate
Out[3]:
array([[0.        , 1.        ],
       [0.70710678, 0.70710678]])
```

summary: linalg.solve: Unclear error when using assume_a='her' with real matrix
description:
My issue is about an obscure error that happens when using `scipy.linalg.solve(a,b, assume_a='her')` with a being a real matrix.
While raising an exception seems logical, the one that is raised makes it harder to diagnose the problem in user code.
(personally, when I first encountered the error, I went to check if the lapack/blas libraries were correctly installed/linked)

#### Reproducing code example:
<!-- 
If you place your code between the triple backticks below, 
it will be rendered as a code block. 
-->

```
import numpy as np
import scipy.linalg as spl
a = np.array([[0,1,2],[1,3,4],[2,4,6]])
a2 = np.asarray(a, dtype=complex)
b = np.array([7,8,9])

spl.solve(a,b, assume_a='sym')   # success: expected behavior
spl.solve(a2,b, assume_a='her')  # success: expected behavior
spl.solve(a2,b, assume_a='sym')  # success: expected behavior: this is a different assumption
spl.solve(a,b, assume_a='her')  # error, see below
```

#### Observed behavior (Error message) :

ValueError: LAPACK function dhecon could not be found

```

#### "Expected" behavior(s)
The exception that is raised is (to me, at least) not clear enough about what the user's blunder was.
I see two (mutually exclusive) possibilities:
- `assume_a` is silently replaced by 'sym', because it is the same assumption as 'her' in the case of of a real matrix.
- an exception is raised earlier, clearly pointing out the dtype mismatch

I attached two (draft-state) patches, one for each possibility (at the end of this report)

(personally, I would go with the former solution, which feels more coherent with the documentation of the `spl.pinv` and `spl.pinvh` functions, although I do not know what would truly be preferred for the project)

#### notes
- both patches were tested with the minimal example given
- I did not (yet) check other functions for similar problems

#### two (mutually exclusive) patches:
patch 1 (draft): silently correct the user's mistake
```
diff --git a/scipy/linalg/basic.py b/scipy/linalg/basic.py
index d673d823c..db0a9ee93 100644
--- a/scipy/linalg/basic.py
+++ b/scipy/linalg/basic.py
@@ -169,6 +169,10 @@ def solve(a, b, sym_pos=False, lower=False, overwrite_a=False,
     if assume_a not in ('gen', 'sym', 'her', 'pos'):
         raise ValueError('{} is not a recognized matrix structure'
                          ''.format(assume_a))
+
+    # for a real matrix, describe it as "symmetric", not "hermitian" (lapack doesn't know what to do with real hermitian matrices)
+    if assume_a == 'her' and not np.iscomplexobj(a1):
+        assume_a = 'sym'

     # Deprecate keyword "debug"
     if debug is not None:
```

+++ b/scipy/linalg/basic.py

         rcond, info = gecon(lu, anorm, norm=norm)
     # Hermitian case 'hesv'
     elif assume_a == 'her':
+        if not np.iscomplexobj(a1):
+            raise ValueError('input a, containing real values, '
+                             'cannot be assumed to be hermitian ("her"). '
+                             'did you mean to assume it is symmetric ("sym")?')
         hecon, hesv, hesv_lw = get_lapack_funcs(('hecon', 'hesv',
                                                  'hesv_lwork'), (a1, b1))
         lwork = _compute_lwork(hesv_lw, n, lower)
