Packages
========

The packages provided here are loosely based on the debian upstream packages with some modifications to make them more usable as non-default pythons and on ubuntu.  As such, the packages follow debian's patterns and often do not include a full python distribution with just `apt install python#.#`.  Here is a list of packages that may be useful along with the default install:

- `python#.#-dev`: includes development headers for building C extensions
- `python#.#-venv`: provides the standard library `venv` module
- `python#.#-distutils`: provides the standard library `distutils` module
- `python#.#-lib2to3`: provides the `2to3-#.#` utility as well as the standard library `lib2to3` module
- `python#.#-gdbm`: provides the standard library `dbm.gnu` module
- `python#.#-tk`: provides the standard library `tkinter` module

Third-Party Python Modules
==========================

Python modules in the official Ubuntu repositories are packaged to work with the Python interpreters from the official repositories. Accordingly, they generally won't work with the Python interpreters from this PPA. As an exception, pure-Python modules for Python 3 will work, but any compiled extension modules won't.

To install 3rd-party Python modules, you should use the common Python packaging tools.  For an introduction into the Python packaging ecosystem and its tools, refer to the Python Packaging User Guide:
https://packaging.python.org/installing/

summary: BUG: sparse: fix DIA.setdiag issue
description:
#### Reference issue
Issue was identified in gh-14004.

#### What does this implement/fix?
When DIA.setdiag() gets a short values array, it only stores the minimum needed to represent the matrix. This can lead to errors later when trying to assign a full-length values array to the same diagonal, as the offset already exists but the backing data isn't large enough.

summary: BUG: Raise exception for inconsistent WAV header
description:
#### Reference issue
Closes https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/13988

#### What does this implement/fix?
Files with a contradictory nBlockAlign field were still being opened,
but with the wrong interpretation of the data.

Example:

    nSamplesPerSec = 0x0000AC44 = 44100 Hz
    nAvgBytesPerSec = 0x00015888 = 88200 bytes per second
    nBlockAlign = 0x0004 = 4 bytes per sample

But nAvgBytesPerSec should equal nSamplesPerSec * nBlockAlign

summary: BUG: Fix root bracketing logic in Brent's method (issue #13737)
description:
The check, f(a)*f(b) < 0, to determine if the interval [a, b]
brackets a root, can fail when the product overflows/underflows.
The modified check is:
sgn(f(a))*sgn(f(b)) < 0, where sgn(x) denotes the sign of x.

Closes #13737

#### Reference issue
<!--Example: Closes gh-WXYZ.-->
fix a part of #12271

#### What does this implement/fix?
As reported in #12271, `minimize` with Powell method has an issue of max function call validation.
The reason for this issue is that `minimize_powell` check the max function call here once a loop:
https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/fbcfba22f2e4f89510f0bc1e24591a6b91204378/scipy/optimize/optimize.py#L3018-L3019
But, `_linesearch_powell` might evaluate the function multiple times.
To fix the issue, I create a new wrap function `_wrap_function_with_validation` which counts function evaluation and raises an exception when function evaluation reaches the maximum value.
We should check other methods have the same issue or not, but this PR only focuses on fixing the issue of Powell method.

summary: reprodcibility of scipy.sparse.linalg.svds
description:
`scipy.sparse.linalg.svds` sometimes gives slightly different results when calling it for the second time. It is not easy to reproduce this behavior for me. I need to use a special input array that I uploaded here: https://sharing.crt-dresden.de/index.php/s/zkgBd6MQj2hd2zq/download 

The data I uploaded is single cell data. So far, I didn't manage to create a random sparse matrix showing the same issue.

I do run the code below in a Jupyter Lab notebook. It is important that I restart the Python kernel and run the code. Then, the reproducibility issue will happen. If I run the code again, without restarting the kernel, successive calls usually give the same result.

I came across the issue when using scanpy, where `svds` is used to do principal components analysis (https://github.com/theislab/scanpy/issues/1749). 

#### Reproducing code example:
<!-- 
If you place your code between the triple backticks below, 
it will be rendered as a code block. 
-->

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.sparse import load_npz
from scipy.sparse.linalg import LinearOperator, svds

X = load_npz('X.npz')
np.random.seed(42)
v0 = np.random.rand(2700)

def linear_operator(X):
    mu = X.mean(0).A.flatten()[None, :]
    mdot = mu.dot
    mmat = mdot
    mhdot = mu.T.dot
    mhmat = mu.T.dot
    Xdot = X.dot
    Xmat = Xdot
    XHdot = X.T.conj().dot
    XHmat = XHdot
    ones = np.ones(X.shape[0])[None, :].dot

    def matmat(x):
        return Xmat(x) - mmat(x)

    def rmatvec(x):
        return XHdot(x) - mhdot(ones(x))

    XL = LinearOperator(
        matvec=matvec,
        dtype=X.dtype,
        matmat=matmat,
        shape=X.shape,
        rmatvec=rmatvec
    )
    return XL


XL = linear_operator(X)


_, s0, _ = svds(XL, solver='arpack', k=50, v0=v0)
_, s, _ = svds(XL, solver='arpack', k=50, v0=v0)
print(np.array_equal(s0, s))

print(s)

summary: BUG: sokalmichener appears to incorrectly apply weights
description:
The code and results for the sokalmichener distance metric appears not to apply weights to all the factors.

I've been writing gpu versions of the distance metrics, and noticed inconsistent results when comparing my sokalmichener values to the scipy ones.

Reading the code, I believe the problem is that the weights are not being applied to the `ntf` and `nft` values:

[distance.py:1582](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/5ab7426247900db9de856e790b8bea1bd71aec49/scipy/spatial/distance.py#L1580):

```python
        w = _validate_weights(w)
        ntt = (u * v * w).sum()
        nff = ((1.0 - u) * (1.0 - v) * w).sum()
    (nft, ntf) = _nbool_correspond_ft_tf(u, v)
```

You can see that the weights `w` are being applied to `ntt` and `nff`, but not passed in to the `ntf`/`nft` calculation.

If this is compared to the `sokalsneath` function immediately below:

```python
        w = _validate_weights(w)
        ntt = (u * v * w).sum()
    (nft, ntf) = _nbool_correspond_ft_tf(u, v, w=w)
```
It superficially seems clear that `w=w` should be passed in to the `_nbool_correspond_ft_tf` function to apply weights.

## Test case:

Here's my worked test case, that shows the issue (It's possible I've misunderstood something here, apologies if so):

```python
from scipy.spatial.distance import sokalmichener

#from: | 1 |   | 0 |
#to:   | 1 |   | 1 |
#weight|   | 1 |   | 0.2
ntf =    0 * 1 + 0 * 0.2
nft =    0 * 1 + 1 * 0.2
ntt =    1 * 1 + 0 * 0.2
nff =    0 * 1 + 0 * 0.2

expected =  2 * (nft + ntf) / (ntt + nff + 2 * (nft + ntf))

print(expected)
assert expected - 0.2857143 < 1e-6
actual = sokalmichener([1, 0],[1, 1], w=[1, 0.2])
assert actual - expected < 1e-6, actual    # fails
```

summary: ENH: stats: improve efficiency of / fix bug in exact permutation t-test
description:
#### Reference issue
gh-4824 ([this comment](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/4824#pullrequestreview-560611611))
Prompted by gh-13263

#### What does this implement/fix?
gh-4824 added a random permutation, two-sample t-test. The t-statistic of the observed data `a` and `b` is compared against a (typically approximate) distribution of the t-statistic under the null hypothesis formed using random permutations of the data. When the number of random permutations requested exceeds the number of distinct permutations, an exact test (using every distinct permutation, each exactly once) is performed. 

*TL-DR punchline*:
The same "exact" p-value can be obtained more efficiently using combinations instead of permutations. Incidentally, this also fixes a bug.

*Detailed punchline*:
The distribution of the t-statistic under the null hypothesis was formed by repeatedly:

- pooling (concatenating) the observations in _a_ and _b_
- randomly permuting the list of pooled observations
- partitioning the permuted list into new samples _a'_ and _b'_ of the same lengths as _a_ and _b_, respectively
- computing the t-statistic of _a'_ and _b'_ 

The "exact" test follows the same approach, using each possible permutation exactly once. This is inefficient: many permutations result in partitions with the same elements in _a'_ (and _b'_) in different orders, but the t-statistic is independent of the order of data within _a'_  and _b'_. Consequently, the same t-statistic is calculated many times.

More precisely, the current "exact" test forms a distribution of the test statistic under the null hypothesis with `factorial(na + nb)` elements (t-statistic values), where `na` and `nb` are the lengths of `a` and `b`, respectively. Distinct values in this distribution are repeated `factorial(na) * factorial(nb)` times. We can get the same p-value more efficiently by generating the distribution under the null hypothesis without all the repetitions:

- pooling (concatenating) the observations in _a_ and _b_
- choosing a combination _a'_ of the elements from the list of pooled observations with the same length as _a_
- forming a set _b'_ containing the remaining observations
- computing the t-statistic with _a'_ and _b'_ 

That is, we form the distribution under the null hypothesis using all distinct partitions of the pooled observations - but now we use only one permutation of each partition rather than all possible permutations.

I refactored code from gh-13263 into a generator function to do this.

#### Additional information
This exposed a subtle bug in the original implementation. 

With perfect arithmetic, the same value of the t-statistic would be calculated regardless of the order of elements within *a'*. This is not always true with floating-point arithmetic. 

The p-value is computed by comparing the observed value of the t-statistic against the distribution of the t-statistic under the null hypothesis. When this comparison is performed with exact `>=` or `<=` comparisons, tiny differences in t-statistic values in the distribution can lead to substantial differences in the p-value. 

The second commit reveals this bug. The third commit will show that the bug is fixed when tolerances are added to the comparisons. The use of combinations instead of permutations ensures that none of these inexact duplicate t-statistic values are generated, so the fourth commit will get rid of the old permutation method (and tolerances on comparisons) in favor of the combination method.

summary: BUG: invgauss.cdf should return the correct value when `mu` is very small.
description:
Currently `invgauss.cdf` returns NaN when mu is too small. This is due to `exp(1 /mu)` blowing up when mu is small (the docs say that this happens for values smaller than 0.0028).
https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/fc77ea19923c39618547b4033a9185dd8a3afcc1/scipy/stats/_continuous_distns.py#L3504-L3509

In the expression evaluatating the CDF, the term `_norm_cdf(-fac*(x+mu)/mu)` is zero when mu is very small, so that the CDF evaluates to 1 due to the term `_norm_cdf(fac*(x-mu)/mu)` being approximately 1 for very small `mu`.

I believe that returning `nan` instead of 1 is not the best approach to handle the overflow. The overflow of `exp` does not practically affect the final value of the cdf is cases when `mu` is very small because `_norm_cdf(-fac*(x+mu)/mu)` is zero anyway.
#### Reproducing code example:
```python
In [1]: import numpy as np

In [2]: from scipy.stats import invgauss

In [3]: rng = np.random.RandomState(1)

In [4]: mu = rng.uniform(0., 0.01, size=5)

In [5]: mu
Out[5]: 
array([4.17022005e-03, 7.20324493e-03, 1.14374817e-06, 3.02332573e-03,
       1.46755891e-03])

In [6]: invgauss.cdf(0.4, mu=mu)
/home/scipy/scipy/stats/_continuous_distns.py:3508: RuntimeWarning: overflow encountered in exp
  C1 += np.exp(1.0/mu) * _norm_cdf(-fac*(x+mu)/mu) * np.exp(1.0/mu)
/home/scipy/scipy/stats/_continuous_distns.py:3508: RuntimeWarning: invalid value encountered in multiply
  C1 += np.exp(1.0/mu) * _norm_cdf(-fac*(x+mu)/mu) * np.exp(1.0/mu)
Out[6]: array([ 1.,  1., nan,  1.,  1.])
```

I played around with handling the overflow by setting the value of `exp(1/mu)` to the largest double and then the remainder of the function evaluates to the "correct" value, which is 1.

```python
In [4]: mu = np.random.uniform(0., 0.01, size=5)

In [5]: invgauss.cdf(0.4, mu=mu)
Out[5]: array([1., 1., 1., 1., 1.])

In [6]: mu
Out[6]: array([0.0006815 , 0.00685858, 0.00949644, 0.00324687, 0.00621239])

In [7]: rng = np.random.RandomState(1)

In [8]: mu = rng.uniform(0., 0.01, size=5)

In [9]: mu
Out[9]: 
array([4.17022005e-03, 7.20324493e-03, 1.14374817e-06, 3.02332573e-03,
       1.46755891e-03])

In [10]: invgauss.cdf(0.4, mu=mu)
Out[10]: array([1., 1., 1., 1., 1.])
```

Here is the code snippet:
https://github.com/scipy/scipy/compare/master...zoj613:invgauss

I was wondering what does everyone think regarding changing the current behavior of the function.


```

```
Looking at the [latest documentation](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.binned_statistic_2d.html), I read the following describing how the statistic argument can be a user-defined function:
> function : a user-defined function which takes a **1D array** of values, and outputs a single numerical statistic. This function will be called on the values in each bin. Empty bins will be represented by function([]), or NaN if this returns an error.

Evidently this isn't the correct behavior. Looking at the source code I see the culprit:
```
def _create_binned_data(bin_numbers, unique_bin_numbers, values, vv):
    """ Create hashmap of bin ids to values in bins
    key: bin number
    value: list of binned data
    """
    bin_map = dict()
    for i in unique_bin_numbers:
        bin_map[i] = []
    for i in builtins.range(len(bin_numbers)):
        bin_map[bin_numbers[i]].append(values[vv, i])
    return bin_map
```

summary: BUG: stats: Fix exponnorm.cdf and exponnorm.sf for small K
description:
The CDF and SF for exponnorm include the term

    np.exp(expval) * _norm_cdf(x - invK)

where

    invK = 1.0 / K
    expval = invK * (0.5 * invK - x)

If K is small, the expression `exp(expval)` will overflow.  This
is a bug, because the other term in the product, `_norm_cdf(x - invK)`,
will be extremely small when K is small, compensating for the large
value in `exp(expval)` and resulting in a value that can be represented
with 64 bit floating point.

To fix this, the logarithms of the two terms are computed, and the
sum is exponentiated.  That is, the product is replaced with

    np.exp(expval + _norm_logcdf(x - invK))

Closes gh-13428.

description:

#### What does this implement/fix?
In `scipy.interpolate.LSQBivariateSpline`, which calls the Fortran subroutine `surfit` as `dfitpack.surfit_lsq` via F2PY, pad both of the knot arrays to the size demanded by the Fortran routine. This fixes the memory error when the sizes of the input knot arrays are different.

An additional test is added that explicitly set the knot arrays to be unequal lengths. The input sizes in the test are also larger than the typical ones we've had so far.

PR #12287 added support for reading arbitrary-bit-depth WAVs, but the code doesn't consider big-endian WAVs, and doesn't work as expected on big-endian platforms due to the use of native-byte-order data-types. This change fixes that.

summary: BUG: stats: Don't raise ZeroDivisionError in _unequal_var_ttest_denom
description:
When both standard deviations given to ttest_ind_from_stats were Python
floating point zeros and the parameter equal_var was False, the private
function _unequal_var_ttest_denom would raise a ZeroDivisionError.  The
code that raised the exception is wrapped in a np.errstate context
manager to catch such errors, but that context manager does not catch
an exception if it is raised by the division of Python floats.

The fix is to convert the inputs of ttest_ind_from_stats to NumPy arrays
before doing any calculations.  Then the exception raised by the
calculation in _unequal_var_ttest_denom will be caught by the context
manager.

Closes gh-6409.

summary: BUG,MAINT: Ensure all Pool objects are closed
description:
#### Reference issue
I noticed this pytest failure in #13249 due to a `multiprocessing.Pool` object not being closed:
https://dev.azure.com/scipy-org/SciPy/_build/results?buildId=9613&view=logs&j=e177c0b2-361c-5cee-6783-4418e98d3ffa&t=663e3bfe-bbaf-5419-7ee8-d9a433818df8&l=671

#### What does this implement/fix?
The main fix is in the `_perm_test` helper from `stats.multiscale_graphcorr` which uses a `MapWrapper` without closing it. Changing to a `with` statement ensures the pool is closed properly.


I also audited for other cases where `Pool` or `MapWrapper` was being misused. `quad_vec` has a chance of leaking the pool if an exception is thrown between `MapWrapper` creation and the actual `with` statement. Moving construction into the `with` fixes that. I also updated a few benign instances of `try-finally` to use `with` just for readability.

#### Additional information
Before #13161, the unclosed `Pool` warning was being hidden by the `__del__` method closing the pool. So, that PR has helped catch this bug which is nice.

summary: Handle cval correctly for ndimage functions with complex-valued inputs
description:
#### Reference issue
closes gh-13248 

#### What does this implement/fix?
The fix here is to use the real component of `cval` when filtering the real component of the image and the imaginary component of `cval` when filtering the imaginary component of the image.

There is also a separate fix for a segfault that could occur if the new interpolation mode, 'grid-constant', was passed to one of the ndimage.filters functions. For the filter purposes there are no non-integer locations and so 'grid-constant' and 'constant' are equivalent.

#### Additional information
New tests were added to validate the expected behavior (there were no existing tests for complex inputs with non-zero `cval`)

This fix will need to be backported to the 1.6.x branch

summary: ndimage: improper cval handling for complex-valued inputs
description:
The complex-value support added in gh-12725 and gh-12812 for **1.6.0rc1** does not handle non-zero `cval` correctly for modes 'constant' or 'grid-constant'.

For example if `cval=1.0` the actualy computation will end up using `cval=1.0 + 1.0j` since the current implementation processes the real and imaginary components independently with the same `cval` argument. 

#### Reproducing code example:

```Python
import numpy as np
import scipy.ndimage as ndi
ndi.shift(np.ones(6, dtype=np.complex64), shift=2, mode='constant', cval=3.0)
```

```array([3.+3.j, 3.+3.j, 1.+0.j, 1.+0.j, 1.+0.j, 1.+0.j])  # note 3.+3.j instead of 3.0 in the initial values```

The same thing happens for ndimage.filters functions

#### Scipy/Numpy/Python version information:
SciPy 1.6.0rc1

summary: tgsen uses an output argument for computing a default argument
description:
tgsen uses `lwork=max(2*m*(n-m),1)` as default argument (for the complex case) where `integer intent(out) :: m`. I assume this means that lwork will always be 1, which is usually insufficient. m is the amount of eigenpairs that will be selected (which may be larger than the amount of nonzeros in the select array in the non-complex case).

Note that the same issue exists for the non-complex case, but this is less visible, since the default is set to `lwork=max(MAX(4*n+16,2*m*(n-m)),1)`, so this includes `4*n+16`.

#### Reproducing code example:

```
@pytest.mark.parametrize('dtype', DTYPES)
def test_gges_tgsen(dtype):
    seed(1234)
    atol = np.finfo(dtype).eps*100

    n = 10
    a = generate_random_dtype_array([n, n], dtype=dtype)
    b = generate_random_dtype_array([n, n], dtype=dtype)

    gges, tgsen = get_lapack_funcs(('gges', 'tgsen'), dtype=dtype)

    result = gges(lambda x: None, a, b, overwrite_a=False, overwrite_b=False)
    assert_equal(result[-1], 0)

    s = result[0]
    t = result[1]
    q = result[-4]
    z = result[-3]

    if dtype in COMPLEX_DTYPES:
        assert_allclose(s, np.triu(s), rtol=0, atol=atol)
        assert_allclose(t, np.triu(t), rtol=0, atol=atol)

    assert_allclose(q @ s @ z.conj().T, a, rtol=0, atol=atol)
    assert_allclose(q @ t @ z.conj().T, b, rtol=0, atol=atol)

    result = tgsen(select, s, t, q, z)
    assert_equal(result[-1], 0)

    s = result[0]
    t = result[1]
    q = result[-9]
    z = result[-8]

    if dtype in COMPLEX_DTYPES:
        assert_allclose(s, np.triu(s), rtol=0, atol=atol)
        assert_allclose(t, np.triu(t), rtol=0, atol=atol)

    assert_allclose(q @ s @ z.conj().T, a, rtol=0, atol=atol)
    assert_allclose(q @ t @ z.conj().T, b, rtol=0, atol=atol)
```

 ** On entry to ZTGSEN parameter number 21 had an illegal value
```

The wrapper for `dgejsv` in `scipy.linalg.lapack` (cp. #11354) seems to have troubles with the transpose (even if deep copies are used). If `dgejsv` is called on an array that had been transposed, it overwrites it. This does not happen for the the *untransposed*.

summary: BUG: stats: fix bug in spearmanr nan propagation
description:
As @urimerhav posted in gh-12411, `spearmanr` with `nan_policy="propagate"` intends to create logical indices of the rows (or columns, depending on axis) that contain nans, perform the calculations, then nan-out the appropriate rows and columns in the output. However, the code:
```
np.isnan(a).sum(axis=axisout)
```
sums the _number_ of nans along the axis rather than returning the logical array that can be used for indexing. The solution is to use `any` rather than `sum`.

summary: BUG: signal: `ss2tf` incorrectly truncates output to integers.
description:
A [question on stackoverflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/65010384/differing-results-in-scipy-vs-matlab-transfer-functions) demonstrates a bug in `scipy.signal.ss2tf`.  The input arrays are
```
A = [[0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1], [-3, -4, -2]]
B = [[0], [0], [1]]
C = [[5, 1, 0]]
D = [[0]]
```
When computing `num, den = ss2tf(A, B, C, D)`, the expected value of `num` is `[0, 0, 1, 5]`, but `ss2tf` returns `[0, 0, 0, 4]`.

From my answer to the question:

> When `ss2tf` creates an array to hold the numerator, it uses the data types of the inputs to determine the data type of the numerator array. In your case, the values are all integers, so the data type of the numerator is integer. However, the coefficients for the numerator are the result of a floating point calculation, and therefore are subject to loss of precision. When the computed values are copied into the numerator array, those values are truncated to integers. In your example, that results in a large error. When I reproduce the floating point calculation of the numerator, I get `[0.0, 0.0, 0.9999999999999947, 4.999999999999995]`, and when those values are copied into the integer array, the result is `[0, 0, 0, 4]`.

We can fix this by ensuring that the output data type for the numerator array is floating point.

summary: scipy.stats.binom_test / binom.sf return incorrect values for large x and n
description:
[scipy.stats.binom.sf](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.binom.html#scipy.stats.binom) and [scipy.stats.binom_test](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.binom_test.html) returns incorrect values for large inputs.  The bounds on the inputs is not documented, and similar functions in other libraries (e.g. R's `binom.test`) do not have this problem.

#### Reproducing code example:

```
>>> np.seterr(all='warn')
{'divide': 'warn', 'over': 'warn', 'under': 'ignore', 'invalid': 'warn'}
>>> scipy.stats.binom_test(1e7, 2e7, 0.5, 'greater')
0.5094024848633918
>>> scipy.stats.binom_test(1e8, 2e8, 0.5, 'greater')
0.6860874231168742
>>> scipy.stats.binom_test(1e9, 2e9, 0.5, 'greater')
0.8854076875623922
>>> scipy.stats.binom_test(1e10, 2e10, 0.5, 'greater')
nan
```

#### Error message:

None.

#### Expected behaviour:

All calls in the repro example should return a value near 0.5.  For example, in R:

```
> binom.test(1e7, 2e7, 0.5, 'greater')$p.value
[1] 0.5000892
> binom.test(1e8, 2e8, 0.5, 'greater')$p.value
[1] 0.5000282
> binom.test(1e9, 2e9, 0.5, 'greater')$p.value
[1] 0.5000089
> binom.test(1e10, 2e10, 0.5, 'greater')$p.value
[1] 0.5000028
```

#### Notes:

Internally, for the "greater" alternative, scipy calls `binom.sf(x - 1, n, p)`, which then calls `scipy.special.bdtrc(floor(x), n, p)`.  This forwards to [Cephes' bdtrc](http://www.netlib.org/cephes/doubldoc.html#bdtrc), according to scipy's docs.

We can verify that the bug lies within `bdtrc`:

```
>>> scipy.special.bdtrc(1e10, 2e10 - 1e10 + 1, 0.5)
nan
```

Non-broken implementations of the regularized incomplete beta function (such as TensorFlow's `tf.math.betainc`) will return the expected value (0.5).

This also affects anything else that calls `bdtrc`, including `binom.sf`.  There may be a case that `bdtrc` is Working as Intended (because the documentation is explicit that it's just a wrapper for Cephes' buggy implementation), but I think for `binom.sf` and `binom_test` it's clear that there is at least a documentation bug if not an opportunity to make things better.

I think there are 4 viable solutions, in what I think is most-preferred to least-preferred:

1. File a bug with Cephes and wait for them to fix it, documenting the breakage in the meantime.
2. Use a normal approximation in `binom.sf` when "k" and "n" are large (perhaps checking that "p" isn't too biased).  Fortunately the circumstances when `bdtrc` breaks usually coincide with when this approximation is good. :)
3. Implement a regularized incomplete beta function within scipy that isn't broken, instead of using Cephes.
4. Claim this is Working as Intended, but document the limitation.

I'm happy to send Pull Requests given some direction about which of the choices above to go with.

#### Scipy/Numpy/Python version information:
```
>>> import sys, scipy, numpy; print(scipy.__version__, numpy.__version__, sys.version_info)
1.5.4 1.19.4 sys.version_info(major=3, minor=6, micro=8, releaselevel='final', serial=0)
```

summary: BUG: sparse: fix inner indexed assignment of a 1d array
description:
Fixes gh-12857.

For an expression like `A[:3, 0] = np.ones(3)`, the logic in `__setitem__` produces the following canonicalized indexing arrays:
 - `i`: column vector `[[0, 1, 2]].T`
 - `j`: row vector `[[0,0,0]]`

The issue is that we would then try to broadcast the new values (`x`) against `i`, creating a 3x3 array. By checking whether a broadcast is necessary, we can avoid some extra work and prevent corner cases like this one.

`scipy.ndimage.median` can give an incorrect result under some circumstances when the input is of integer type. This is due to potential integer overflow or boolean addition within the median calculation in one code path.

#### Reproducing code example:
<!-- 
If you place your code between the triple backticks below, 
it will be rendered as a code block. 
-->
```Python
import numpy as np
import scipy.ndimage as ndi

ndi.median(np.asarray([1, 1], dtype=np.bool), labels=np.ones((2,)), index=[1,])
```
gives `array([0.5])` when one would expect `array([1.0])`

Setting either `labels` or `index` to None does give the expected value of 1.0.

As a second example,
```Python
import numpy as np
import scipy.ndimage as ndi

ndi.median(np.asarray([65, 70], dtype=np.int8), labels=np.ones((2,)), index=[1,])
```
gives `array([-60.5])` when one would expect `array([67.5])`
Changing to `dtype=np.int16` here avoids integer overflow and gives the expected result


#### Additional Information
The root cause of this is boolean or integer array addition in this line:
https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/353f2563896ba3d077f4a4a19b938a7ff101db21/scipy/ndimage/measurements.py#L896

summary: BUG: Scipy Sparse slice indexing assignment Bug with zeros
description:
<!-- 
Thank you for taking the time to file a bug report. 
Please fill in the fields below, deleting the sections that 
don't apply to your issue. You can view the final output
by clicking the preview button above.
Note: This is a comment, and won't appear in the output.
-->

My issue is about assigning to a subset of a sparse matrix, taking assigned values from another sparse matrix, in particular the case where the other matrix is all zeros. 

#### Reproducing code example:
<!-- 
If you place your code between the triple backticks below, 
it will be rendered as a code block. 
-->

```python
from scipy.sparse import lil_matrix
from numpy.random import rand, seed
seed(30)
# behaviour as normal
A = lil_matrix((10, 10))
A[0, :2] = rand(2)

B = lil_matrix((10, 10))
B[0, :] = rand(10)
B[0, 0:3] = A[0, 0:3] # at least 1 nonzero works
print(A[0, :3].todense())
print(B[0, :3].todense())

# strange behaviour
B = lil_matrix((10, 10))
B[0, :] = rand(10)
tmp = A[0, 2:4]
B[0, 2:4] = tmp # this is all zero and doesn't change B

print(A[0, 0:4].todense())
print(B[0, 0:4].todense())
```
This code is adapted from the usage information page for scipy.sparse. It is a bit contrived, since here I explicitly know that I am assigning zeros, but in my actual case where I spotted this is, this was a trick to work out.
The code doesn't produce an exception, but it doesn't produce expected behaviour - this is the output:
```
[[0.64414354 0.38074849 0.        ]]
[[0.64414354 0.38074849 0.        ]]
[[0.64414354 0.38074849 0.         0.        ]]
[[0.51817635 0.76685511 0.93385014 0.08970338]]
```
In the first two lines where we had a nonzero element, we have the same thing. In the second two, we would expect that the final two entries in each row would be zero, but they are not.

This issue is only present in the case where the assignment is a slice, not a scalar. As best  I can tell, this is because for the scalar case, the equivalent of ```tmp``` in the above is a numpy float, but in the slice case it's a sparse matrix (lil_matrix in this case)

I had a look with a debugger, following the ```B[0, 2:4] = tmp``` line back, the issue seems to be in ```scipy/sparse/_index.py```
around line 112 where the size is checked, found to be zero since all elements are zero and then no assignment is done. Commenting this check out locally seems to "fix" the problem, but probably has unforeseen consequences.

#### Scipy/Numpy/Python version information:
```
1.5.2 1.19.1 sys.version_info(major=3, minor=7, micro=7, releaselevel='final', serial=0)
```

description:
<!--

Note that we are a team of volunteers; we appreciate your

Again, thanks for contributing!
-->

#### Reference issue
<!--Example: Closes gh-WXYZ.-->
closes gh-1323
closes gh-8131
closes gh-8465
resolves: scikit-image/scikit-image#1585

resolves part of gh-2640
   - 'reflect' and and the new 'grid-wrap' have correct boundary behavior (the name `grid-wrap` was suggested by @stefanv: https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/206#issuecomment-408326019)
   - modes 'constant' and 'nearest' can still be improved in a subsequent PR

@rgommers, @stefanv: this is the second PR related to the NumFOCUS proposal.

#### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->
This PR makes a number of improvements to boundary handling in ndimage. This is related to prior discussions in #206, #2640, and #8465. It is probably easiest to review the commits in order rather than all at once.

This PR fixes boundary handling when mode='reflect' and introduces a new mode, `'wrap-grid'` that behaves according to the description of wrap in the docstring. Prior to this PR, the requested `mode` is only used when wrapping the current coordinate into the original signal range:
https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/d866f8342a1c0f1fb8175460e520ea264bca1ca5/scipy/ndimage/src/ni_interpolation.c#L409). 
However, `mirror` mode was then [always used for other coefficients involved in the interpolation](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/d866f8342a1c0f1fb8175460e520ea264bca1ca5/scipy/ndimage/src/ni_interpolation.c#L426-L439). This was done because previously, only mirror boundary conditions had been implemented for spline orders > 1. However as of #8537, we also have boundary conditions implemented for reflect and wrap cases.

For backwards compatibility, I have kept the current `wrap` as-is, but am not sure if we want to keep it or should just replace it with the new behavior. I also added a `grid-mirror` alias for the name `reflect` as suggested in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/206#issuecomment-408326019, but I'm not sure if we really want/need to add that.

#### Additional information
<!--Any additional information you think is important.-->

Prior to this PR, boundary handling for both 'reflect' and 'wrap' were not as expected for any spline order.

The boundary handling for `mode='nearest'` was also improved slightly for order >1, but I intend to revisit this again and see if the remaining error can be avoided in a subsequent PR. mode='constant'` will also be revised in a future PR.

## Updated example based on the one given in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/2640#issuecomment-554873759
The figure in the comment is still a match to current master. The new behavior after this PR is shown below for order=3:

![compare_to_padded_order3](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6528957/91190372-81dc5a80-e6c1-11ea-99e7-50e706b8310a.png)


Note that unlike on current master the existing `'reflect'` mode and the new `'grid-wrap'` mode match the case where explicit padding/extension of the signal was performed prior to calling the interpolation.

#### Reference issue
<!--Example: Closes gh-WXYZ.-->

closes gh-12758

#### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

Avoid the loss of precision for small arguments by using the Taylor series for small x.

#### Additional information
<!--Any additional information you think is important.-->

At small arguments, `erf(x) = 2/\sqrt{\pi} (x - x^3 / 3 + ...)`, so we only keep the linear term for `|x| < 1e-7` and then the inverse function `erfinv(x) = x * \sqrt{\pi} / 2`.

#### Reference issue
Closes #12654: from discussion on issue, "scipy.stats.combine_pvalues seems to work incorrectly with method='mudholkar_george'"

#### What does this implement/fix?
"According to the original article approx_factor should be equal to np.sqrt(nu / (nu - 2)) / scipy.pi * np.sqrt(3 / len(pvalues)), not np.sqrt(nu / (nu - 2))"

p-values are now calculated correctly as described in the [article](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/235117023_The_Logit_Statistic_for_Combining_Probabilities_-_An_Overview)

#### Additional information
I've made a few attempts at contributing in the past but was unsuccessful, so please review carefully. I did the following: 

1. followed the scipy dev guide 
2. removed the old unit test that was comparing an incorrect value and added a new one 
3. All tests pass in test_stats.py 
4. Let me know what I need to do to credit @M1kss for the code - he adjusted the method and I edited / tested; I'm not sure what the usual protocol is here.

summary: BUG: use special.sindg in ndimage.rotate
description:
This makes `np.all(a == ndimage.rotate(ndimage.rotate(a, 180), -180))` be `True` when a has integral dtype.

Even if this isn't a perfect fix, there is no reason not to use `sindg` instead of converting to radians.  And getting this case correct is why these functions exist.

fixes gh-12543.

summary: rv_sample expect bug
description:
#### Reference issue

Reported at Stackoverflow, https://stackoverflow.com/questions/63199792/why-do-scipy-stats-rv-discrete-mean-and-expect-show-unexpected-difference

`rv_sample.expect` gives wrong answers in some cases.


#### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

`rv_discrete.expect` iterates over the support of the distribution, assuming that it contains contiguous integers (This is baked into discrete distributions, save `rv_sample`.)  Thus chunked iteration in  `_expect` gives wrong results if the sample points  `xk` are not equidistant with `self.inc == 1`. Furthermore, the bug is masked by a shortcut in `_expect` for small lengths of `rv_sample.xk`

So this PR just reimplements `_expect` for `rv_sample`.

#### Additional information
<!--Any additional information you think is important.-->

Also remove an `_argcheck` call which is no longer needed now that `_argcheck` is not allowed to set `.a` and `.b`

summary: Warnings are not filtered in csr_matrix.sum()
description:
Dear scipy community,

suffering for one hour on the application side, I realized that there is a noteworthy bug in scipy.

```python
import scipy.sparse as sps
import warnings

counts = [1]
row_ids = [0]
column_ids = [1]


csr_matrix = sps.csr_matrix((counts, (row_ids, column_ids)),
                            shape=(1, 2),
                            dtype=int)


for i in range(5):
    s = csr_matrix.sum()
    warnings.warn("This message should be printed only once", UserWarning)
```

Warnings:
```
/home/ulianych/PycharmProjects/elephant/ignored/scipy_warn_bug.py:17: UserWarning: This message should be printed only once
  warnings.warn("This message should be printed only once", UserWarning)
/home/ulianych/PycharmProjects/elephant/ignored/scipy_warn_bug.py:17: UserWarning: This message should be printed only once
  warnings.warn("This message should be printed only once", UserWarning)

```

As the message says, the warning should be printed only once. Citing the official python documentation,

> Repetitions of a particular warning for the same source location are typically suppressed.

Adding `warnings.simplefilter("module", UserWarning)` or `once` doesn't help either.

Note that if you comment out the line where the sum of a matrix is computed, the warning is printed only once as it should.

summary: eigvalsh inconsistent eigvals= subset_by_index=
description:
A low-priority inconsistency, eigvals= subset_by_index= in linalg/decomp.py eigvalsh --

 """ eigvalsh eigvals= vs. subset_by_index= in scipy 1.5
        doc: eigvals : tuple (lo, hi), optional
                *Deprecated by ``subset_by_index``
        code:
            def eigvalsh( ... eigvals=None, subset_by_index=None ... )
                return eigh( ... subset_by_index=eigvals )  # <-- oops

    a quick fix (corrected 29 june):
            if eigvals is None:
                eigvals = subset_by_index  # an alias, either one works
            return as above          

        and change the doc, why deprecate ?
            eigvals is an alias for subset_by_index
    """
    import platform
    import sys
    import numpy as np
    import scipy
    from scipy.linalg import eigvalsh

    print( "numpy %s  scipy %s  python %s  plaform %s " % (
        np.__version__, scipy.__version__ , sys.version.split()[0], platform.platform() ))

    A = np.diag( np.arange( 10 ))
    e = eigvalsh( A, eigvals=[0, 3] )
    print( "eigvalsh( A, eigvals= ):", e )

    e = eigvalsh( A, subset_by_index=[0, 3] )
    print( "eigvalsh( A, subset_by_index= ):", e )  # all, subset_by_index ignored


Output:

summary: scipy.stats.spearmanr mishandles nan variables with "propogate"
description:
`scipy.stats.speramnr` tries to see which variables have a nan value and nan-out their results in the output matrix. This is seen in [line 4215](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/ac49c61d92fc11719b4a6a1ad09145ee607dd76f/scipy/stats/stats.py#L4215)

`variable_has_nan = np.isnan(a).sum(axis=axisout)`


 Unfortunately right now it accidentally applies a SUM where it should be applying ANY. As a result, the indexing vector isn't boolean as expected, but instead an integer based off of the number of nan entries. 

So let's say variable 2 has 3 nan entries, the result will be that variable *3* gets replaced with a nan, and not 2. 

Proposed fix:

`variable_has_nan = np.isnan(a).sum(axis=axisout)` -> `variable_has_nan = np.isnan(a).any(axis=axisout)`

summary: BUG: Iteration index initialisation is wrong in scipy.optimize.linesearch.scalar_search_wolfe2
description:
My issue is about the initialisation of the iteration index in the [line search function which produces a step size satisfying the strong Wolfe conditions (`scipy.optimize.linesearch.scalar_search_wolfe2`)](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/v1.4.1/scipy/optimize/linesearch.py#L411).

#### Reproducing code example:
The algorithm comes from page 60 of [Wright and Nocedal, 'Numerical Optimization', 1999](https://pages.mtu.edu/~struther/Courses/OLD/Sp2013/5630/Jorge_Nocedal_Numerical_optimization_267490.pdf).

The index should be initialised a `i=1` but in scipy it is `for i in xrange(...)` which starts at 0. This has an impact on the chosen path the algorithm takes. Specifically, the condition on line 430 sometimes wont be True and an alternative route will be chosen,

``` python
if (phi_a1 > phi0 + c1 * alpha1 * derphi0) or \
           ((phi_a1 >= phi_a0) and (i > 1)):
    ...
```

I noticed this when implementing the line search for JAX where I use scipy's implementation for a unittest. I was inspecting why I woud sometimes get a difference. The purpose of the `i>1` part is so that that statement is true only when at least one iteration has occured. In scipy's implementation, it implies that it's true only when at least two iterations have occured. This might cause extra function evaluations, or simply make the line search fail in worse case. Quite a simple fix though.

#### Scipy/Numpy/Python version information:
```
1.4.1 1.18.4 sys.version_info(major=3, minor=6, micro=10, releaselevel='final', serial=0)
```

summary: ValueError 'k exceeds matrix dimensions' for sparse.diagonal() when 0 in sparse.shape

It can require adding special cases/conditionals around `.diagonal()` calls, such as https://github.com/stellargraph/stellargraph/pull/1378.

Minimal:

```python
import scipy.sparse as sps
import numpy as np
m = sps.csr_matrix((0, 0))
print(np.diag(m.todense()).shape) # (0,)

m.diagonal() # ValueError: k exceeds matrix dimensions

summary: BUG: avoid recomputing in scipy.optimize.optimize.MemoizeJac
description:
Fixes #11868

This PR adapts scipy.optimize.optimize.MemoizeJac to also cache the
function result when the gradient is requested before the function value
(which is the case when using HessianApproximationStrategy, as,
e.g., the case in `minimize(method='trust-constr')`). Previously, the
function value was only cached when the value of the function was requested,
but not when the gradient was requested.

I also added tests that make sure the values are cached correctly. I wasn't
sure how to name the test file for `scipy/optimize/optimize.py` since there
was already a `scipy/optimize/tests/test_optimize.py` testing the module itself.
I went for `scipy/optimize/tests/test__optimize.py`. Let me know if you prefer something else.

summary: Function always evaluated twice when using HessianUpdateStrategy with function that returns value and gradient
description:
<!-- 
Thank you for taking the time to file a bug report. 
Please fill in the fields below, deleting the sections that 
don't apply to your issue. You can view the final output
by clicking the preview button above.
Note: This is a comment, and won't appear in the output.
-->

[scipy.optimize.minimize](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.optimize.minimize.html) supports handing a function that computes both function value and jacobian and returns them as tuple. I noticed that when using `method='trusts-constr'`, this results in the function always being called twice in a row for exactly the same value. After digging into the code, I noticed that the function is wrapped into `MemoizeJac` which should avoid calling the function multiple times, but this doesn't work in this case:

#### Reproducing code example:
```
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize._differentiable_functions import ScalarFunction
from scipy.optimize._minimize import MemoizeJac
from scipy.optimize import BFGS

def test_fun(x):
    print("eval", x)
    return np.sum(x**2), 2*x

fun = MemoizeJac(test_fun)
jac = fun.derivative
hess = BFGS()

x0 = np.array([1.0, 0.5])
# the following line will evaluate the function once
diff_fun = ScalarFunction(fun, x0, (), jac, hess, None, None) 

# the following line will evaluate the function _twice_
diff_fun.fun(x0+0.1)

# as will this line
diff_fun.fun(x0+0.2) 
```
#### Error

`test_fun` should have been called only once per function evaluation, but except for the initialization of ScalarFunction, it is always called twice. I think I already found the source of this: `MemoizeJac` assumes that the function value is always requested before the gradient value and therefore only checks in the gradient call for existing results. However, if the hessian is a `UpdateHessingStrategy`, calling `diff.fun` first requests the gradient in order to do a hessian update and only then requests the function value. And in this case, `MemoizeJac` does not cache the function result.

#### Scipy/Numpy/Python version information:
```
numpy: 1.3.3 scipy: 1.17.4 system: sys.version_info(major=3, minor=6, micro=8, releaselevel='final', serial=0)
```

summary: BLD: fix build with gfortran 10
description:
#### Reference issue
Closes: gh-11611

#### What does this implement/fix?

Gfortran 10 forbids by default certain nonstandard constructs, which breaks Scipy build in a few places (see https://gcc.gnu.org/gcc-10/porting_to.html). The feature must be explicitly enabled by adding compiler flag `-fallow-argument-mismatch` where necessary.

Implement pre-build hooks that add the flag when necessary, and use it in the four places we need it (arpack, id_dist, slsqp, nnls).

Also, extend the pre-build hook machinery to support hooks in `build_clib` (needed for arpack) and multiple hooks.

summary: L-BFGS-B error message always reports 20 line search iterations
description:
If the L-BFGS-B minimization method terminates abnormally due to the maximum number of line search iterations, it displays this message:

```
 Line search cannot locate an adequate point after 20 function
  and gradient evaluations.  Previous x, f and g restored.
 Possible causes: 1 error in function or gradient evaluation;
                  2 rounding error dominate computation.
```

I want to note that it says "after 20 function...evaluations" regardless of how many evaluations it did. 20 is the default value of `maxls`, but if you change it to something else, say 40, the message still says 20, which is confusing. summary: documentation of scipy.spatial.HalfspaceIntersection: wrong method to compute feasible point
description:
I am reading the docs of:
https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.spatial.HalfspaceIntersection.html

the example states an algorithm for computing a feasible point for the halfspace intersection algorithm by setting up a linear problem. However, the algorithm uses

res = scipy.optimize.linprog(c, A_ub=A, b_ub=b)

to solve the problem, which additionally adds an implicit constraint x>0. This works in the example as the solution indeed produces positive values only. But in the code example below, flipping the one constraint in the example around to produce negative x-values will result in the wrong solution.

The correct way is to explicitly disable all box-constraints:
res = scipy.optimize.linprog(c, A_ub=A, b_ub=b, bounds = (None,None))

#### Reproducing code example:
```
from scipy.spatial import HalfspaceIntersection
from scipy.optimize import linprog
import numpy as np

halfspaces = np.array([[1, 0., 0.], # example uses -1
                       [0., -1., 0.],
                       [2., 1., -4.],
                       [-0.5, 1., -2.]])

norm_vector = np.reshape(np.linalg.norm(halfspaces[:, :-1], axis=1),
    (halfspaces.shape[0], 1))
c = np.zeros((halfspaces.shape[1],))
c[-1] = -1
A = np.hstack((halfspaces[:, :-1], norm_vector))
b = - halfspaces[:, -1:]
#wrong:
res = linprog(c, A_ub=A, b_ub=b)
print(res.x)
#correct
res = linprog(c, A_ub=A, b_ub=b, bounds = (None,None))
print(res.x)

```


#### Scipy/Numpy/Python version information:
1.4.1 1.17.4 sys.version_info(major=3, minor=7, micro=0, releaselevel='final', serial=0)

summary: BUG: fix use of is in DE callback
description:
#### Reference issue
No referenced issue -- I'm happy to create one if needed

#### What does this implement/fix? 
While using differential evolution I found that the callback function did not work if the result was not identical (in the `is` sense) to True.

Eg:
```
def mycallback(param, convergence=0.):
   return (np.array([1]) == 1)[0]
```
Will *not* halt differential evolution.


This commit changes the condition to be identical in the `==` sense. Critically, this allows the
user to work with numpy arrays in an intuitive way, where previously they could not, because the
numpy True wasn't equivalent in the `is` sense to the python True.

This commit also includes a test to demonstrate the bug.

#### Additional information
I wonder a little why the code was `is True` to begin with. My theory is that it is to make it more difficult to accidentally return True by returning a  floating point value. It seems like it's better to keep optimizing than to stop immediately, just because the user accidentally returned some non-zero float from the callback.

Another reason might be to help programmers avoid a situation where they return an array and get `ValueError: The truth value of an array with more than one element is ambiguous. Use a.any() or a.all()`. But I think it's better to just fail this way and let them fix the bug. However, this might create bugs in existing code where the callback returns an array.

Another option here is to check for whether this is an instance of `np.bool_`, eg:

```
if ... and isinstance(result, (bool, np.bool_)) and result:
```

Let me know what makes most sense and I'll update the commit.

summary: scipy.stats.zipf doesn't implement zipf distribution
description:
<!-- 
Thank you for taking the time to file a bug report. 
Please fill in the fields below, deleting the sections that 
don't apply to your issue. You can view the final output
by clicking the preview button above.
Note: This is a comment, and won't appear in the output.
-->

Scipy implements the zeta distribution for scipy.stats.zipf instead of the zipf distribution.  There is no such thing as scipy.stats.zeta, so this affects users who wish to utilize either distribution.  The current scipy.stats.zipf should be renamed to scipy.stats.zeta and the zipf function should be implemented instead.  

#### Reproducing code example:
From `help(scipy.stats.norm.zipf)` the PMF described by the zipf documentation is the PMF for the Zeta distribution, not the Zipf distribution.  
```
class zipf_gen(scipy.stats._distn_infrastructure.rv_discrete)
 |  A Zipf discrete random variable.
 |  
 |  %(before_notes)s
 |  
 |  Notes
 |  -----
 |  The probability mass function for `zipf` is:
 |  
 |  .. math::
 |  
 |      f(k, a) = \frac{1}{\zeta(a) k^a}
 |  
 |  for :math:`k \ge 1`.
 |  
 |  `zipf` takes :math:`a` as shape parameter. :math:`\zeta` is the
 |  Riemann zeta function (`scipy.special.zeta`)
```

#### More Details
See the Wikipedia page for the zipf and zeta distributions.  Wikipedia calls it out as "Zipf distribution is related to the zeta distribution, but is not identical."
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zipf%27s_law
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeta_distribution

summary: Callback function doesn't give the same value as the one being displayed by SciPy SLSQP
description:
Hi,

I'm working with the SLSQP method from scipy.optimize.minimize to solve constrained problems. I'm really interested in getting the objective function value and the x value (x being the vector of parameters) at each iteration. I'm using the "disp=True" and "iprint=2" options in order to see the results during the optimization, but I couldn't find how to get all these values into arrays automatically (to plot them, for example), so I'm also using a callback function which adds the x value and the objective value to 2 lists at each iteration.

I would expect this callback function to save the same values as those being displayed during the optimization, but it's not the case. I've tried printing the objective value at each function evaluation and I've seen the callback function saves the last evaluation. However, I don't understand what value is being displayed. I first thought it was the smallest evaluation, but sometimes it's not.
The difference between the callback value and the displayed value is often very little at last iteration but I've come across a case where the last callback x is different from the scipy.optimize.minimize result. In this case, I have seen another problem : the cost function is being evaluated after the last iteration (so no callback on these evaluations, but the result depends on these evaluations).

I tried to reproduce it on a smaller code :

```
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import scipy.optimize as spo


def f(x):
    m = np.array([0.2,0.15,0.3])
    xx = (x-m)
    return ((1-xx[0])**2+100*(xx[1]-xx[0]**2)**2 + xx[2])**2 #**1 for second issue, if ftol=1e-6

### init
x0 = np.zeros(3)
Obj0 = f(x0)

### Objective function
def Obj(x):
    y = f(x)/Obj0  #  (Rosenbrock function + x2)**2
    print('Obj : ',y)
    return y


### Inequality Constraint
def Cons1(x): # srqt(x1**2+x2**2-x1*x2+3*x3**2) < C --> 1-sqrt(...)/C >0
    C = 4.3
    return 1-np.sqrt(x[0]**2+x[1]**2+3*x[2]**2-x[0]*x[1])/C

cons = {'type':'ineq',
        'fun':lambda x: Cons1(x)}

### Callback function
XX = [x0.copy()]
FF = [Obj(x0)]
def CB(x):
    global XX, FF
    XX += [x.copy()]
    FF += [Obj(x)]
    print('CB :  ',FF[-1])

    
### Bounds
boundmin = -5*np.ones_like(x0)
boundmax = 5*np.ones_like(x0)
bounds = spo.Bounds(boundmin, boundmax)

#%% OPTIMIZATION

res = spo.minimize(Obj, x0, callback=CB, method='SLSQP',constraints=[cons], options={'ftol': 1e-6, 'disp': True,'maxiter': 100, 'iprint': 2,'eps':1.e-6},bounds=bounds)


#%% Plotting the results
plt.figure()
plt.plot(FF)
```

The two first iterations give an objective value of 5e7 and 1e3 with the callback function, whereas 1 and 5.7e-2 are displayed. The constraints are verified at each evaluation (except for the one at 5e7). At iterations 3 and 4 (and maybe others), the displayed value is bigger than the callback value (so it's not the smallest value that is being displayed).
If I set the power to 1 in the f function (it changes the objective function), there is an evaluation after the last iteration.

I have the following questions : what exactly is displayed by scipy.optimize.minimize SLSQP ? Since callback values and displayed values are different, how to save the **displayed** values into arrays (or lists) ?
Why are some evaluations made after the last iteration ?

Thanks a lot for your help and answers, and for reading my long question.

P.S. : if it helps, I'm working with Scipy 1.1.0 version.

summary: BUG: directed_hausdorff distance on sets u and v when u is a subset of v
description:
When `u` and `v` are two sets with `u` being a subset of `v` we should get:

`directed_hausdorff(u, v, seed=0) = (0, index_of_any_point_from_u, index_of_the_same_point_from_v)`

While the distance is returned correctly, the indices for the points witnessing this distance are not guaranteed to be correct. For example,

`directed_hausdorff([(0,0)], [(0,1), (0,0)], seed=0)` return correct answer of `(0.0, 0, 1)`
but `directed_hausdorff([(0,0)], [(0,1), (0,0)], seed=1)` returns incorrect `(0.0, 0, 0)`. 

This is due to strict inequality, `cmin > cmax`, in line 66 of [_directed_hausdorff definition](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/v1.4.1/scipy/spatial/_hausdorff.pyx), as this prevents reassignment of `j_ret` (and `i_ret`) from its default value of `0` (because `cmax=cmin=0` on all `i` iterations in the case of `u` being a subset of `v`). 

To fix this, either the `cmin > cmax` could be changed to `cmin >= cmax` or it could be checked in the beginning if `u` is a subset of `v`.

summary: BUG: fix floating-point literal comparisons under C99
description:
Floating point literals under gcc -std=c99 -mfpmode=387 (default on i386
platform) can have 'excess precision' with 80-bit floating point instead
of 64-bit.

Add explicit casts to force some of the literals to the same precision
as the precision of the variables they are compared against.

(The code changes here are no-ops on platforms such as amd64 where gcc defaults to fp math with the precision of the data type, but not e.g. on 386 where the fpu can have wider precision. See FLT_EVAL_METHOD, which also affects constants.)

Fixes: most of the failures in gh-11270 (except the optimize linprog ones)

summary: BUG: special: fix behavior for `rgamma` zeros
description:
#### Reference issue
Closes https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/11315.

#### What does this implement/fix?
Get the zeros of `rgamma` on the negative real axis correct.

#### Additional information
The implementation of `rgamma` for real arguments tries to detect
zeros showing up in the sin factor of the reflection formula, but
since it uses `sin(NPY_PI * w)` instead of a proper `sinpi`
implementation it fails to detect them due to rounding errors. Fix
that by using `sinpi` instead. This requires moving our `sinpi`
implementation out of Cython and into C; of course you can call Cython
functions from C, but that doesn't work with our current ufunc setup.

Also tweak the mpmath test for `rgamma`-it overrides the mpmath
`rgamma` to explicitly return `inf` for large negative arguments, but
now that we are getting the zeros correct we will eventually return
only zero.

summary: fix docs & behavior for mode sequences in ndimage filters
description:
#### Reference issue
<!--Example: Closes gh-WXYZ.-->
closes #9632

#### What does this implement/fix?
A few of the `scipy.ndimage.filters` docstrings suggest that a sequence of modes is supported when it is not. This PR fixes this and also adds a more informative error for cases like that reported in #9632.

The underlying C code in `scipy.ndimage` does not support a sequence of modes. Sequence of mode support is currently only possible when the filtering operation can be applied as a separable sequence of 1d filters.

#### Additional information

`convolve`, `correlate`, `median_filter` and `generic_filter` are not separable and just needed a doc fix to not suggest that a sequence of modes is allowed.

`minimum_filter` and `maximum_filter` can support a sequence of modes when the filter footprint is separable, so I have just added a Notes section explaining that. I added a more informative `RuntimeError` when a sequence is provided and this is not the case. 

`rank_filter` and `percentile_filter` are also generally not separable, so I have updated the docstring to reflect that. However, for these two, there are specific cases where they call either `minimum_filter` or `maximum_filter` internally. In those edge cases, a sequence of modes is possible, as the modes argument just gets passed on to `minimum_filter` or `maximum_filter`. I think it is probably best not to document that as supported behavior, but I did not explicitly disallow it here.

summary: BUG: Rework the scaling in the ks_2samp two-sided exact test.
description:
Rework the scaling in stats.py:_compute_prob_inside_method() based on
magnitide of biggest value rather than presuming that the binomial
will be sufficient to keep dynamic range within needs.

#### Reference issue
Closes gh-11184

#### What does this implement/fix?
Some intermediate computations were implicitly assuming that applying terms of a binomial factor would keep the results within a double's dynamic range.  For large sample sizes this wasn't always true.

Rescale the intermediate values when they reach 2**900 and apply the binomial and undo the scaling at the end of the computation.

summary: Sparse matrix constructor data type detection changes on Numpy 1.18.0
description:
There is some change in Numpy 1.18.0 with regard to integer data type selection. (This is currently causing refguide-check failures on master.)

On Numpy 1.18.0 we get
```
>>> scipy.sparse.csc_matrix(np.array([[1]])).dtype.type
<class 'numpy.longlong'>
>>> scipy.sparse.csc_matrix(np.array([[0]])).dtype.type
<class 'numpy.int64'>
```
whereas on 1.17.4 both result to `<class 'numpy.int64'>`. The integer type sizes are the same (`sizeof(long long) == sizeof(npy_int64)`), so this is some subtlety about which one gets picked by the csc_matrix constructor. Interestingly, `np.array()` picks always the `numpy.int64` one, so this might more probably be issue in scipy.sparse.

description:

Note that we are a team of volunteers; we appreciate your
patience during the review process.

Again, thanks for contributing!
-->
#### What does this implement/fix?
In the shortest paths function(with method == 'auto') there was a bug in counting edges for dense graph representation. (non-existent edges marked with np.inf were counted, while existing edges with weight 0 were skipped). This could lead to the selection of a suboptimal algorithm.
I fixed it by splitting it into two cases:
* For dense masked representation I counted number of non-masked elements.
* For dense array representation I changed elements equal to inf and NaN to 0 and then I counted number of elements bigger than 0.

I also got rid of the warnings that popped up when non-existent edges were marked by NaN. Thus this fixes #5144.

Fixes a bug with `sos2zpk`:
```
>>> from scipy.signal import butter, sos2zpk

Another option would be to cull the "effectively zero" ones. Not sure which is better, but the "effectively zero" case is pretty easy for users to do with something like `mask = np.isclose(z, 0., atol=1e-14)`, setting `atol` as required or however else they want to do it. And in the current pattern, you can check to see which sections were effectively first-order by reshaping the output, so it might actually be more usable than a reduced version (?).

summary: MAINT: lbfgsb func_and_grad should use copy
description:
There is an issue in `_minimize_lbfgsb` in `optimize/lbfgsb.py`. When the minimizer is [requested](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/master/scipy/optimize/lbfgsb.py#L345) to call the function and gradient it should be providing a copy of `x` to the user, but instead passes `x` directly.

I first noticed this issue in #10673 with [this failing test](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/master/scipy/optimize/tests/test_optimize.py#L360).
The test keeps a trace of all the `x` arrays passed to the objective function. However, if you get the existing code to print out the trace all the entries are the same. This shouldn't occur, `x` should be changing as the minimization proceeds, converging on the solution.

The tracer is appending the `x` array to a list. However, the `x` array is being modified in-place by `_lbfgsb.setulb`. Thus the trace just ends up as a list of the same array appended time and time again.
Here the solution is to fix the tracer in the test by making it do a copy when it appends to the list, remove the exact trace requested in `test_l_bfgs_b`, and also to change `_minimize_lbfgsb` to pass a copy of `x` when is asks for evaluation of `func_and_grad`.

summary: BUG: optimize: ensure solvers exit with success=False for nan returns
description:
#### Reference issue

#### What does this implement/fix?

Several of the minimzers have termination checks of the type `while err_est > tol: do_stuff`, but that will terminate also when `err_est` is nan. Fix this by adding checks after termination that termination was not due to nan.

summary: BUG: optimize/slsqp: deal with singular BFGS update
description:
#### Reference issue
Closes: gh-9640

#### What does this implement/fix?

SLSQP can run to singular BFGS updates, which it doesn't handle, and may exit with nan outputs and successful exit code. To avoid this, do the most trivial thing and just reset the matrix. This might not lead to convergence, but gets rid of false successful exits.

Also fix suspicious convergence check in the case where SLSQP exits due to too many bfgs resets when encountering positive directional derivative. This looks like a bug where it was forgotten that after gotoing to label `255` the variable `h3` does not contain the constraint violation, because the associated initialization code of the basic convergence check (at label `240`) is skipped.

Moreover, fix SLSQP linalg function behavior when encountering nans. The fix is simply rewriting positivity guard `if (x <= 0)` as `if (.not.(x > 0))` to guard also against x nan.

The linalg changes are no-ops if there are no nans, and with nans generally give error exits. The BFGS update tweak is only triggered in cases where the code previously divided by zero. The SLSQP exit-on-too-many-resets check is also a corner case. So there should be no impact in non-problematic cases.

summary: BUG: `coo_matrix` does not validate the `shape` argument.
description:
In a [stackoverflow question,](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/55060950/sparse-matrix-hstack-getting-error-regarding-subscriptability) a user created a `coo_matrix` as follows:

    a = coo_matrix([0, 11, 22, 33], ([0, 1, 2, 3], [0, 0, 0, 0]))

Apparently they neglected to put the values and indices into a tuple, and instead of creating an array with shape `(4, 1)`, they got an array with shape `(1, 4)`:

```
In [4]: a = coo_matrix([0, 11, 22, 33], ([0, 1, 2, 3], [0, 0, 0, 0]))

In [5]: a.shape
Out[5]: (1, 4)

In [6]: a.A
Out[6]: array([[ 0, 11, 22, 33]])
```

The problem is that the call shown above is equivalent to

    a = coo_matrix(arg1=[0, 11, 22, 33], shape=([0, 1, 2, 3], [0, 0, 0, 0]))

and clearly that `shape` value is not valid.  The call should generate a `ValueError` instead of silently ignoring the `shape` argument.  Note that the shape is completely ignored--the following does not generate an error:

    b = coo_matrix([[0, 1], [2, 3]], shape='foo')

-----

summary: BUG: skip deprecation for numpy top-level types
description:
Deprecation decoration of type objects is more likely to cause problems
than for functions, so don't do it. Deprecation of plain functions is
likely enough to result to deprecation warnings in most cases.

This would likely be important to fix for Scipy 1.4.0, as otherwise we break
the backward compatibility here.

E.g. the array scalar type objects are often used in `dtype=` arguments
and possibly compared with other scalar objects, and our deprecation
decoration currently breaks that:
```
>>> import scipy, numpy as np
>>> assert scipy.array([1,2,3], dtype=scipy.float64).dtype == np.float64
__main__:1: DeprecationWarning: scipy.array is deprecated and will be removed in SciPy 2.0.0, use numpy.array instead
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/home/pauli/prj/scipy/scipy/scipy/_lib/deprecation.py", line 14, in call
    return fun(*args, **kwargs)
TypeError: data type not understood
>>> assert scipy.float64 == np.float64
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
AssertionError
```
It's possible to do the decoration so that the above still works, via
subclassing with metaclass, but it's hard to be sure that covers everything
necessary. Since deprecation of functions already likely generates deprecation
warnings in suspect code, it's probably enough.

summary: BUG: Fix signal.unique_roots
description:
#### Reference issue

#4915

#### What does this implement/fix?
`signal.unique_roots` is supposed to find unique roots among a list of real or complex roots, meaning that roots closer to each other than `tol` are considered identical. 

The previous implementation relied on passing through the sorted list of roots. It works for real roots in 1-dimensional space, but doesn't work for complex roots which live in 2-dimensional space where sorting doesn't help at all.

I use `cKDTree` for finding neighboring roots and the time complexity `O(n * log(n) + sum(multiplicity))`. Note that `sum(multiplicity)` occurs because I use `query_pairs` and it might be `O(n**2)` when each root close to all other roots. 

I think `sum(multiplicity)` can be eliminated by more careful usage of `cKDTree`, but it will make the code lengthier and probably slower for typical normal cases.

*Update*: I tweaked the code to make the complexity solid `O(n * log(n))`, due to implementation it works about 10 times slower when each root is unique, however it doesn't choke when there are ~n repeated roots. I think this is a preferable tradeoff.

summary: BUG: make C-implemented root finders work with functools.lru_cache
description:
#### Reference issue
Closes #10846.

#### What does this implement/fix?
C-implemented root finders in `scipy.optimize` raise `SystemError` when passed a function wrapped with `functools.lru_cache`. This is because when calling C-implemented root finders we create the tuple of arguments to pass to the underlying function once, and modify only the first entry on subsequent calls. This breaks when the argument tuple is stored internally by `functools.lru_cache`.

My fix is to instead construct a new argument tuple each time the underlying function is called.

As this change has the potential to slow down the root finders I ran the following benchmark:

```
from scipy.optimize.zeros import bisect

def f(x):
    return x

# The slowest root finder
%timeit bisect(f, -1, 1 + 1/3)
```
on `master` this gives:
```4.78 µs ± 277 ns per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 100000 loops each)```
on this branch this gives:
```5.18 µs ± 204 ns per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 100000 loops each)```

which represents an 8% slowdown. I think that this is pretty much an upper bound on the slowdown, as the function we're finding the root of is trivial, and this is using the most naive root-finder (i.e. it does the least amount of work per function call).

#### Additional information
This bug is present in older versions of Scipy, but I have applied the fix on top of `master`. I could not find any information on Scipy's policy regarding how far back bugfixes should be applied. Let me know if I should apply this fix to one of the `maintenance/*` branches instead.

summary: scipy.signal.signaltools._fftconv_faster has incorrect estimates
description:
My issue is about the function `scipy.signal.signaltools._fftconv_faster`. The function has a logical error, causing most convolutions to use fft when the direct method would save a large factor.

Code example, showing that `_fftconv_faster` returns that fft is faster even when multiplying by a scalar kernel, when the signal is large enough.
```
>>> from scipy.signal.signaltools import _fftconv_faster
>>> _fftconv_faster(np.empty(1), np.empty(1000000), "full")
True
```

Here is the impact in timing on a lenovo yoga 920, intel core i7 8th gen, 16gb ram, running Ubuntu 18.04:
```
>>> import numpy as np
>>> from scipy.signal import convolve
>>> h = np.random.randn(1)
>>> x = np.random.randn(1000000)
>>> %timeit convolve(x, h, method="direct")
714 µs ± 14 µs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1000 loops each)
>>> %timeit convolve(x, h)
70.2 ms ± 1.34 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10 loops each)
```

The automatic run, which chooses fft, is slower by a x100 factor.

The root cause for this is the incorrect estimate for the number of multiplications in the direct convolution algorithm. This is line 506 in v1.3.1, and 497 of the latest commit [8a3e9fa] as of writing this issue:
```
direct_time = (x.size * h.size * _prod(out_shape))
```

The correct direct computation time is actually:
```
direct_time = min(x.size, h.size) * _prod(out_shape)
```

The big oh constants, in the tens of thousands, were probably calculated as a ratio to the incorrect estimate. So a fix to the direct estimate will need to be accompanied by a recalculation to the constants.

summary: Deprecate complex kernel for `expi`?
description:
Typically the exponential integral `Ei` (`special.expi`; see https://dlmf.nist.gov/6.2#E5) is only defined for real values. This is because it doesn't have a proper analytic continuation around the negative real axis. If you want a complex version of `Ei`, then you should just use `E1` (`special.expi1`; see https://dlmf.nist.gov/6.2#E2), which has a branch cut on the negative real axis.

`specfun` however, defines a complex version of `Ei`, which we wrap. It just naively extends the relation `Ei(-x) = -E1(x)` to the complex plane. This leads to a discontinuity between the real/complex implementations around the negative real axis:

```
>>> import scipy.special as sc
>>> sc.expi(-1 + 1e-12j)
(-0.21938393439552062+3.1415926535894254j)
>>> sc.expi(-1 - 1e-12j)
(-0.21938393439552062-3.1415926535894254j)
>>> sc.expi(-1)
-0.21938393439552062
```

This is not how we typically handle things in special (e.g. `loggamma` and `gammaln` are distinct functions for exactly this reason). Can we get away with deprecating the complex variant of `expi` (`exp1` is a drop-in replacement), or at this point are we stuck with just documenting the strangeness?

summary: BUG: ScalarFunction stores original array
description:
There is a bug in `optimize._differentiable_functions.ScalarFunction`, the class is storing the supplied x-array for caching purposes. However, instead of storing a copy it's storing the supplied array. This means that if the supplied array is modified in-place the `ScalarFunction` is evaluating the function incorrectly.

```
>>> from scipy.optimize._differentiable_functions import ScalarFunction
>>> def f(x):
...         return np.sum(np.asarray(x)**2)

>>> x = np.array([1., 2., 3.])
>>> sf = ScalarFunction(f, x, (), '3-point', lambda x: x, None, (-np.inf, np.inf))
>>> x is sf.x
False
>>> sf.fun(x)
14.0
>>> x is sf.x
False
>>> x[0] = 0.
>>> sf.fun(x)
13.0
>>> x is sf.x
True
>>> x[0] = 1.0
>>> sf.fun(x)     # should be 14.0
13.0
>>> sf.x is x
True
```

This PR adds the above test (in the first commit). In subsequent tests the bug in `ScalarFunction` is fixed.

summary: BUG: stats: Formula for the variance of the noncentral F distribution is incorrect.
description:
The formula for `mu2` in `ncf_gen._stats` is not correct.  Currently it is

        mu2 = np.where(dfd <= 4, np.inf, 2*(dfd*1.0/dfn)**2.0 *
                       ((dfn+nc/2.0)**2.0 + (dfn+nc)*(dfd-2.0)) /
                       ((dfd-2.0)**2.0 * (dfd-4.0)))

The terms `(dfn+nc/2.0)` and `(dfn+nc)` are not correct.  They should be `(dfn + nc)` and `(dfn + 2*nc)`, respectively.  This can be checked on the [wikipedia page about the noncentral F distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noncentral_F-distribution), or on [Wolfram's Mathworld article on the noncentral F distribution ](http://mathworld.wolfram.com/NoncentralF-Distribution.html) (In the MathWorld page, be sure to use the formula shown for the central moment μ₂.  There are a couple mistakes on the MathWorld page.  One of them is that the formula shown for σ² incorrectly gives the **raw** second moment instead of the **central** second moment.)

#### Reproducing code example:

For parameters `dfn=2`, `dfd=6`, `nc=4`, the variance should be 42.75, but `scipy.stats.ncf.var(2, 6, 4)` returns 22.5:
```
In [93]: stats.ncf.var(2, 6, 4)                                                                                      
Out[93]: 22.5
```
A quick check of the variance of some large samples agrees with the expected value of 42.75:

```
In [94]: x = stats.ncf.rvs(2, 6, 4, size=10000000)                                                                   

In [95]: x.var()                                                                                                     
Out[95]: 41.57065484486061

In [96]: x = stats.ncf.rvs(2, 6, 4, size=10000000)                                                                   

In [97]: x.var()                                                                                                     
Out[97]: 42.92661339053967
```

#### Scipy/Numpy/Python version information:

```
In [92]: import sys, scipy, numpy; print(scipy.__version__, numpy.__version__, sys.version_info)                     
1.4.0.dev0+30ca45f 1.16.4 sys.version_info(major=3, minor=7, micro=3, releaselevel='final', serial=0)
```

I'm working on a pull request to fix this.

summary: BUG: cKDTree GIL handling is incorrect
description:
I believe #9915 has introduced errors in ```cKDTree``` GIL handling.

Declaring a C++ function ```nogil``` in Cython does not ensure that the GIL is automatically released and reaquired. It only declares that it is allowed to call the function in a nogil context.

Releasing the GIL in Cython is accomplished with a ```with nogil:``` statement. There is no such statement in ```ckdtree.pyx```. Therefore, ```cKDTree``` does not release the GIL and all multithreading code is now defective.

We must either revert #9915 to keep GIL release and exception translation in C++ or fix ```ckdtree.pyx``` to actually release the gil.

Using `scipy.spatial.transform.Rotation.match_vectors` to find the rotation matrix between two sets of vectors, one occasionally gets an incorrect rotation matrix.

The reason is that `match_vectors` uses SVD to find the rotation matrix but does not check if the solution is proper right-handed coordinate system rotation. (see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kabsch_algorithm and references there in)

```python
    d = (np.linalg.det(u) * np.linalg.det(vh)) < 0.0
